Appendix E - Vulnerability Patching Lifecycle

  1. The following time to deploy measurements will be used based on the severity and service type which the vulnerability treatment should be applied too. The time to deploy measurements includes analysis, testing packaging and rollout of vulnerability treatment and define an end to end agreed operating level for the management of vulnerabilities:

Service Type 1-CRITICAL 2-NON-CRITICAL

User access devices such as 5 days 31 days laptops, desktops, virtual desktop instances

Broadband Network Services 14 days 180 days

Internal Services (Excluding 10 days 70 days User Access Devices and Hardware Based Network Appliances)

Internal Services - Hardware 10 days 70 days Based Network Devices

External Services - All types of 5 days 28 days IT Systems and Infrastructure

  1. A vulnerability will be defined 1-CRITICAL if one or more of the following characteristics exist when applied to the supplier's IT Systems and Infrastructure:

a) The vulnerability is remotely exploitable and allows unauthenticated access;

b) The vulnerability does not require any authentication or bypasses normal user authentication (i.e. -- user is not aware of it);

c) The vulnerability directly enables the execution of code on the vulnerable device;

d) Exploit code is either publicly available or existence of an exploit has been detected by other sources;

e) The affected system(s) is in a sensitive area (i.e., Internet facing, Network Security Zone with critical applications);

f) There are no perimeter mitigations and/or no additional internal mitigation in place.

docs.title: Appendix G - Applicable to Telecommunications (Security) Act 2021
Introduction
docs.text:
1. The following requirements apply to all Suppliers considered to be in scope of the Telecommunications Security Act:

a) Where the Supplier has been engaged to support a network, equipment, service or facilities (including equipment vendors, carriers, 3rd party administrators, transit providers, SaaS providers, data centres and colocation providers) on behalf of Community Fibre, the Supplier warrants it shall ensure compliance with the Telecommunications (Security) Act 2021 and associated regulations, measures and oversight in its own right; (M2.06)

b) The Supplier acknowledges and permits that in some circumstances Community Fibre will wish to share details of security issues with other appropriate parties to support the identification and reduction of the risks of security compromises occurring across industry stakeholders in relation to the public electronic communications network or public electronic communications service as a result of things done or omitted by on their behalf (M10.46) and to improve and maintain compliance with legal, regulatory and contractual obligations; and

c) Where security failings are not resolved within a reasonable time frame Community Fibre shall be entitled to deem this a material breach of obligation, not capable of remedy and free to exit any and all contracts with the Supplier without penalty. (M10.15)

docs.title: Equipment Vendors
docs.text:
1. Where the Supplier is providing hardware, software, services, or facilities to Community Fibre that will be used on the Community Fibre fibre or other network, or installed in customer homes / premises, the Supplier must additionally comply with the requirements in this section.

    2. The Supplier must provide Community Fibre with details of any subcontractors that are used to supply Hardware or Software including any major components, services, or facilities (as defined in M10.01) to Community Fibre. This shall include at least the following, and such further information as Community Fibre may require to satisfy the Telecommunications Security Code of Practice requirement shall also be provided prior to the commencement of supply or prior to any changes:

a) name of subcontractor;

b) address of subcontractor's head office;

c) geographical locations in which subcontractor operates; and

d) product or service obtained from this subcontractor. (M10.01)

1.  Where the Supplier is providing any Hardware or Software to
    Community Fibre, they must share with Community Fibre a
    'Security Declaration' \[M10.36\] and any evidence of testing,
    management standards and configuration for enhancing security,
    as required by Community Fibre \[M8.04\], covering how the
    Supplier ensures the production of secure Hardware and Software
    and maintain the security, prior to procurement and through its
    lifetime.

a) The Security Declaration shall include (where applicable) the following:

i. product lifecycle management;

ii. product security management;

iii. protected development and build environments -- including locations of manufacture / assembly;

iv. exploit mitigations;

v. secure updates and Software signing;

vi. Hardware roots of trust and secure boot.

vii. security testing

viii. secure management and configuration; and

ix. vulnerability and issue management -- including process and contact points for bi-directional engagement on vulnerability declaration and remediation. (M10.36)

b) The Security Declaration shall include a record of any differences in process across product lines. (M10.37)

c) The Supplier shall ensure that the Security Declaration is signed off at an appropriate governance level. (M10.38)

d) Where the Supplier makes claim of any of its Hardware or Software achieving any internationally recognised security assessments or certifications, the Supplier shall share with Community Fibre the full findings that evidence such assessment or certification. (M10.39)

e) The Supplier shall adhere to a standard no lower than that expressed within the Security Declaration. (M10.40)

1.  Community Fibre requires the Supplier to share its Security
    Declaration, as defined in the Telecommunications Security Code
    of Practice \[M4.02\] \[M10.36\].

2.  In alignment with National Cyber Security Centre guidance on
    assessing the security of vendors, Community Fibre requires
    evidence from each Supplier of the following elements:

a) risk and security assessments;

b) compliance with security obligations and requirements;

c) support of products / components (if applicable);

d) management of any security incidents / vulnerabilities; and

e) other relevant information.

1.  This evidence will be reviewed by Community Fibre in conjunction
    with the Security Declaration provided by the Supplier (if
    applicable) and any other supporting evidence. (M4.02)

2.  The Supplier must make available or provide access to Hardware,
    Software, services or facilities that Community Fibre needs to
    security test for use in its network, administration or other
    services or data sharing arrangements, and this must be done
    before contract award or on changes to any parameters of the
    contract. Community Fibre will require full cooperation with any
    such testing. The testing shall cover:

a) security functionality (M8.01); and

b) negative testing and fuzzing of all interfaces (M8.02)

1.  Testing of any Hardware or Software must be done by an
    independent subcontractor (not Community Fibre or the Supplier)
    and shall only be accepted if it is repeatable, performed
    independently of the Supplier, and clearly applicable to
    Community Fibre's deployment of the Hardware / Software. (M8.03)

2.  The Supplier will:

a) remove or change all default passwords and accounts on any Hardware or Software that is supplied to Community Fibre and disable all unencrypted management protocols. Where unencrypted management protocols cannot be disabled the Supplier shall assist Community Fibre in limiting and mitigating the use of these protocols as far as possible (M8.06).

b) ensure that all security-relevant logging is enabled on all Hardware and Software and work with Community Fibre to ensure that logs are correctly transferred to the network and security logging systems; (M8.07);

c) ensure that Community Fibre is supplied with up-to-date guidance on how the hardware and / or software should be secured (M10.41).

d) support all hardware and / or software, all subcomponents - including subcontractor supply and support of the same - for the length of the contract. This period and level of support shall be written into the contract (M10.42).

e) provide Community Fibre with details (product and version) of major components and dependencies - including open-source components and components sourced from subcontractors - and the period and level of support (M10.43).

f) ensure that its subcontractors shall prioritise critical security patches over functionality upgrades wherever possible; (M8.08) and shall deliver to Community Fibre critical security patches separately to feature releases, to maximise the speed at which the security patches can be deployed (M10.47); and

g) have a vulnerability disclosure policy which includes, as a minimum, a public point of contact and details around timescales for communication (M10.54).

docs.title: Third Party Administrators and Managed Service Providers
docs.text:
1. Where access is given to administer Community Fibre's network, equipment, service or facilities or to sensitive data, the Supplier must additionally comply with the requirements in this section.

    2. The Supplier will accept and apply security controls as directed by Community Fibre, which are at least as rigorous as those applied by Community Fibre within its own Systems, equipment, services and facilities. (M10.17) Additionally, employees and contractors working for the Supplier who access the network, equipment, services, or facilities shall notify Community Fibre of any security concerns or flaws in defined access methods.

    3. The Supplier acknowledges Community Fibre must retain control and oversight of the Community Fibre Network and Community Fibre Data. (M10.05) Where any transfers of control, or of Community Fibre Data occur the following restrictions shall apply: (M10.08)

a) The Supplier shall only request, or permit, control of elements of the Community Fibre Network when absolutely necessary. Any transfer of control shall be limited to the necessary and defined purpose.

b) Only remote access methods that have been defined and agreed with Community Fibre, and are owned and operated by Community Fibre, shall be used. (M10.22)

c) The Supplier shall only request, or permit, transfer of Community Fibre Data to their Systems when absolutely necessary. Where a transfer of Data is necessary it shall be through a defined process.

d) The Supplier acknowledges that where network or Community Fibre Data leaves Community Fibre's control, Community Fibre shall contractually require that the Data is protected and will periodically verify the protections that are in place.) This shall include the Supplier ensuring that Data is only visible or accessible to appropriate employees and from appropriate locations. (M10.09)

e) The Supplier shall only use an encrypted and authenticated channel when transferring Community Fibre Data. (M10.10)

1.  The Supplier shall support, as far as appropriate, any security
    audits, assessments or testing required by Community Fibre in
    relation to the security of any Hardware or Software, service or
    facilities used to administer the Community Fibre Network,
    including those necessary to evaluate the security requirements
    documented in the Telecommunications Security Code of Practice.
    (M10.16)

2.  Community Fibre shall retain the right to determine permissions
    of the accounts used to access its network, equipment, services
    or facilities by Third Party Administrators following a defined
    role-based access control model. (M10.18)

3.  The Supplier shall assist Community Fibre in maintaining an
    up-to-date list of all the Supplier's personnel and contractors
    who require access to Hardware, Software, services or facilities
    used to administer the Community Fibre Network, by supplying
    details including role, responsibilities and expected frequency
    of access. Names and account names of any staff or contractors
    who temporarily or permanently cease to require access shall be
    notified to Community Fibre promptly (along with relevant
    dates), so that their access can be appropriately suspended or
    revoked. (M10.20) in line with the Community Fibre joiners,
    movers, leavers policy within 24 hours of the change of status.

4.  The Supplier acknowledges that Community Fibre must ensure it
    retains sufficient in-house expertise and technical ability such
    that it is able to re-tender any managed services agreement at
    any time, and therefore that the Supplier will provide all
    reasonable assistance to ensure Community Fibre is able to
    produce and maintain a plan for moving the provided services
    back in-house or to a different supplier. (M10.19)

5.  The Supplier acknowledges that Community Fibre have the
    contractual right to: Impose security controls on all Supplier
    Personnel who are providing Community Fibre with administrative
    services, including requiring the Supplier to ensure that any
    member of their personnel may at any time, on the demand of
    Community Fibre, have their access revoked and be no longer able
    to access equipment, services or facilities or used to
    administer the Community Fibre Network. (M10.21)

6.  Community Fibre requires the Supplier to:

a) implement:

i. technical controls which will prevent any of the Supplier's clients or their network from adversely affecting any other client or their network; (M10.24)

ii. logical separation within their network to segregate the data and networks of each of the Supplier's different clients; (M10.25)

iii. separation between management environments used for the Supplier's different clients; (M10.26)

iv. security enforcing functions at the boundary between the Supplier's network and Community Fibre's network; (M10.27)

v. technical controls to limit the potential for users or systems to negatively impact more than one of the Supplier's clients; (M10.28)

vi. logically independent privileged access workstations that are not used for any other client; (M10.29)

vii. independent administrative domains and accounts for each of the Suppliers clients; (M10.30)

b) monitor and audit the activities of the Supplier's staff when accessing or administering the Community Fibre Network; (M10.33)

c) obtain, store, retain and make available to Community Fibre on demand, all logs relating to the security of the Supplier's network and Supplier Systems to the extent that such logs relate to access into Community Fibre's network for at least 13 months prior to the request date; (M10.34)

d) ensure that if the Supplier's networks or any of the Supplier Systems, including user endpoints, could impact Community Fibre then they have the same level of testing that Community Fibre applies to its own networks; (M10.35) and without prejudice to the generality of the foregoing:

i. the Supplier shall conduct an annual red teaming event equivalent to TBEST, along with prior testing of major releases / new systems / significant changes to Systems (networks, systems, applications, etc.) based on assessment of security requirements so that all implemented network security functions are tested sufficiently to simulate a competent attacker; and

ii. the testing shall be conducted by an independent external party that has CREST and CHECK certification -- or OSCP / OSCE, CRT / CTL, CRTO or at least five years of experience where the testing is done by an individual.

docs.title: Document Objective
docs.text:
The process description below outlines the steps involved in managing Joiners, Movers, and Leavers (JML) to ensure compliance with ISO27001 standards and maintain information security integrity.

This document meets the following clauses:

  • Information Security Management System BS EN ISO/IEC 27002:2017 -- A.6 People Controls

docs.title: Setting up a new starter
docs.text:
• Recruitment will inform HR Operations once they have offered a new role and candidate has accepted a job offer.

  • Team Tailor will generate notification to Zinc to send out RTW Checks

  • HR Operations will set up a new account in BambooHR once candidate has accepted the job offer and a start date is agreed.

  • HR Operations will setup the new BambooHR account with the following minimum details:

  • Full Name

  • Full Address

  • Phone Number

  • Email Address

  • Hire Date

  • Employment Status effective date

  • Employment status (FTE, Part Time, etc)

  • Job Title

  • Reporting manager

  • Department

  • Division

  • Location

  • Pay Rate

  • Pay type

  • Pay schedule

  • Once this is completed a "hiring packet" is sent to the new employee via BambooHR "Save and Create New Hire Packet". The employee will confirm their details and add the following to their hiring packet:

  • Employee completes home address, email address and phone number

  • mandatory documents to complete are contract and offer letter

  • The Starter/Leaver tracker document shared with Recruitment and IT is updated so that they are informed of new starters, date of role commencing, and so that IT accounts and equipment is arranged on time.

docs.title: New starter reference checking and DBS Checks
docs.text:
• Recruitment will align a candidate in Teamtailor with the necessary Zinc package to carry out further checks.

  • Candidate will be sent a link to complete details for references, Right to Work Checks, Address Checks and DBS checks.

  • HR Operations will obtain at least one reference and have proven attempts that there were attempts to contacts at least one more. This is actioned via Zinc

  • Visa & passport information is verified by Zinc and updated in Bamboo once accepted

  • HR Operations let the recruiter know once all checks have been carried out.

docs.title: Movers
docs.text:
• Departmental leaders will send an email to HR Operations to inform them of a staff member moving into another role.

  • HR Operations will send an offer letter as an addendum to the employees existing employment contract outlining necessary changes to conditions of employment.

  • HR Operations will adjust information in BambooHR as reflected in the new offer letter.

  • HR Operations to send a notification of a staff member's role changing to IT service desk.

  • IT service desk to adjust assigned roles and group membership as required.

docs.title: Leavers
docs.text:
• Email, including a written resignation from the leaver, where obtainable, is sent to HR Operations, where an Acknowledgement Letter is produced and provided to the upcoming leaver.

  • HR complete IT Leavers form with confirmation of leaver date.

  • HR to inform Payroll of leaver's exit date.

Payroll to update ADP and company pension etc. with exit date.

  • IT will contact leaver straight away to arrange collection of any relevant company property, e.g., Mobile, laptop etc.

  • IT Service desk to deactivate all accounts on agreed exit date.

  • Payroll will terminate them in ADP and company pension following their final pay.

Related Policies:

  • CFL-006 - Process Document - Change Management

  • ISP042-Software Development Policy

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text: This document outlines the standardised process for managing software releases to ensure controlled, secure, and efficient deployment of changes to production environments. It addresses ISO 27001 Annex A Control 8.32 (Change Management) by providing clear steps, documentation, and accountability for all release types.

docs.title: Scope
docs.text:
This procedure applies to all software releases within the organisation, including:

  • New features or major enhancements.

  • Code fixes (e.g., bug resolutions).

  • Minor changes such as data updates, script modifications, or queries.

  • Emergency releases.

It covers systems like HOBS and any other production software, including development, testing, staging, and production environments. BAU tasks not involving code or data changes (e.g., monitoring) are not covered by this procedure.

docs.title: Role and responsibilities
docs.text:
Role Responsibilities

Release Manager Oversees the release process; coordinates teams; ensures documentation completeness; schedules releases.

Developer Prepares changes; conducts initial testing; creates release notes and documentation.

Change Owner Validates release notes and overseas the change implementation and reviews the deployment by DevOps Team

Tester/QA Team Performs independent testing; verifies security and functionality.

Change Advisory Reviews and approves releases; assesses Board (CAB) risks and impacts.

Information Security Evaluates security implications; ensures Officer (ISO) compliance with ISO 27001 controls (e.g., 8.29 for testing, 8.32 for changes).

DevOps Team Deploys releases on SIT/UAT/prod Environment and executes rollback if needed.

Operations Team Performs Sanity and Monitors post-release performance

TCS Team (if Provides specialised support for applicable) HOBS-related changes; maintains documentation.

docs.title: Release management process
docs.text: The process follows a structured Software Development Lifecycle (SDLC) with risk-based scaling. All releases must be initiated via a change ticket in Jira.

docs.title: Initiation and planning
docs.text:
• Identify the change type and scope.

  • Create a change ticket with details: description, rationale, affected components, and potential impacts.

  • Conduct an initial risk assessment (qualitative for minor changes; quantitative for major ones) covering security, availability, and business impacts.

  • For HOBS changes: Reference system-specific guidelines.

  • Output: Updated change ticket; preliminary release plan.

docs.title: Development and preparation
docs.text:
• Develop/code the changes in a segregated environment (development branch).

  • For minor changes (e.g., data scripts): Ensure version control and basic peer review.

  • For code fixes: Implement unit tests and integrate with existing codebase.

  • DevOps team move the changes to SIT/UAT from Dev branch.

  • Prepare release artifacts: Binaries, scripts, configuration files.

  • Output: Code committed to GIT Lab repository; initial release notes drafted.

docs.title: Testing and quality assurance (QA)
docs.text:
• Perform testing in isolated environments:

  • Unit/Integration Testing: Automated where possible.

  • Security Testing: Vulnerability scans performed in Aikido tool

  • User Acceptance Testing (UAT): For major releases.

  • Scale by type: Minor changes require basic functional tests; major changes need full regression testing.

  • Document test results, including pass/fail criteria and evidence (e.g., screenshots, logs).

  • Output: Test report attached to change ticket.

docs.title: Review and approval
docs.text:
• Submit for CAB review: Present release documentation, risks, and mitigation plans, Only UAT passed changes are considered.

  • Obtain approvals: Electronic sign-off from relevant roles (e.g., ISO for security).

  • For emergency releases: Use fast-track approval with post-release review.

  • Developer provides prod Notes after peer review and then DevOps team reviews the prod notes and plan accordingly.

  • Output: Approved release plan; scheduled deployment window.

docs.title: Deployment
docs.text:
• Deploy during approved windows as per the release deployment notes (e.g., off-peak hours). Currently release is manually deployed onto servers by DevOps Team. Gitlab CI/CD pipeline is in progress.

  • Follow deployment checklist: Backup production data; implement changes; verify post-deployment.

  • Output: Deployment log, updated system status, Sanity test results.

  • In case of any issue, rollback all the changes according to plan provided by Dev Team.

  • Close the change with Sanity report.

docs.title: Post-release review and closure
docs.text:
• Monitor for issues (e.g., via logging tools) for a defined period (min. 12 hours).

  • Conduct a post-implementation review: Assess success, capture lessons learned.

  • Ops Team will mark the ticket in Monitoring status.

  • Output: Post-release report; updated knowledge base and related tickets in JIRA.

docs.title: Emergency release process
docs.text:
• Bypass non-essential steps (e.g., full testing) with ISO/CAB verbal approval.

  • Complete full documentation retrospectively within 24 hours.

  • Follow all steps of standard CR related to code, testing and deployment process except point 1.

docs.title: Documentation requirements
docs.text:
All releases require formal documentation to ensure traceability and auditability. Use standardised templates stored in a central repository (e.g., Jira or Confluence).

  • Release Note Template (Mandatory for all changes):

  • Change ID/Ticket Number.

  • Description and Type.

  • Risk/Impact Assessment.

  • Development Lifecycle Steps Taken (e.g., \"Developed in dev env; tested via unit tests\").

  • Testing Evidence.

  • Approvals and signoffs.

  • Deployment Details (steps, timestamp, rollback plan).

  • Post-Release Monitoring Results.

  • For Minor Changes (e.g., data queries/scripts): One-page checklist.

  • For Code Fixes/Normal Changes: Detailed report with code diffs and test logs.

  • Retention: Maintain records for at least 2 years or as per legal requirements.

docs.title: Tools and resources
docs.text:
• Ticketing System: Jira

  • Version Control: Gitlab

  • CI/CD Tools: Gitlab

  • Testing Tools: Aikido

  • Monitoring: Datadog, CloudWatch monitoring

docs.title: Risk management and security integration
docs.text:
• Development practices are in alignment with CFL ISP042-Software Development Policy

  • Escalate high-risk releases to senior management.

  • Invoke incident response if issues arise post-release.

**

docs.title: General Information
docs.text:
The purpose of this control is to ensure all information security and privacy requirements are identified and addressed when developing or acquiring applications.

This document meets the following clauses:

  • ISO/IEC 27001:2022 Annex A.8.26 - Application Security Requirements.

docs.title: Policy
docs.text:
We operate public electronic communications networks and services and are subject to UK regulations. Our systems are predominantly hosted on cloud platforms, and we undertake significant bespoke software development. This policy integrates secure-by-design principles into our development lifecycle, referencing our ISP042-Software Development Policy for processes such as secure coding, testing, and deployment. We adopt a systematic approach to application security and privacy by:

  • Classifying information as 'Confidential' or 'Strictly Confidential' in line with the ISP037-Information Classification and Handling Policy

  • Addressing identification, access, authorisation, and segregation through:

  • Identity management to ensure entities are who they claim to be. ISP012-Identity Management Policy

  • Authentication information to ensure \'we know who we are dealing with before we give them information. ISP040-Password Management Policy

  • Privileged access rights. ISP013-Privileged Access Rights Policy

  • A.8.5: Secure authentication.

  • Defining application information and privacy requirements through risk assessment, analysis, and treatment (per ISO 27001:2022 Clause 6.1.2 and 6.1.3).

  • Encrypting services in line with ISP035-Cryptographic Control Policy, considering the information classification. We always encrypt where any Personally Identifiable Information (PII) or sensitive data will be passing over untrusted networks.

  • Managing compliance in line with customer and business requirements and standards for information security.

  • Ensuring that critical services are constantly monitored for attack or undesired activity, with appropriate alerting if anomalous activity is detected.

This policy applies to all in-house developed applications, acquired third-party applications, and cloud-based systems on AWS and Azure.

docs.title: Scope
docs.text:
This policy covers:

  • Bespoke applications developed internally, including web applications, APIs, and backend services.

  • Cloud-hosted systems on AWS (e.g., EC2, S3, Lambda) and Azure (e.g., Virtual Machines, Blob Storage, Functions).

  • Integration with public electronic communications networks.

  • All phases of the software development lifecycle as outlined in ISP042-Software Development Policy, including requirements gathering, design, coding, testing, deployment, and maintenance.

Exclusions: This does not cover hardware-specific security (e.g., routers), which is addressed in separate network security policies.

docs.title: Key principles
docs.text:
To align with the Regulations:

  • Applications must be designed to reduce risks of security compromises, including identifying risks to functions (e.g., whether they handle sensitive data or are security-critical), recording exposures to incoming signals, and ensuring independence from external dependencies (e.g., no reliance on non-UK persons/equipment for risk identification).

  • Applications must protect stored data and functions using technical means appropriate to the data/function (e.g., encryption for sensitive data, access controls for security-critical functions).

  • Adopt a risk-based approach, ensuring proportionality and appropriateness of measures.

  • For third-party components (e.g., AWS/Azure services), assess and mitigate supply chain risks.

  • Integrate logging and monitoring into applications. (Monitoring and Analysis

  • Ensure timely patching of vulnerabilities.

  • Include security testing in development.

docs.title: Application Security Requirements
docs.text:
1. Requirements gathering and risk assessment

  2. Conduct a security risk assessment at the start of any development or acquisition project, identifying \"assessed security risks\" and classifying functions as security-critical if they impact network/service operation.

  3. Document risks in a written record (retained for at least 3 years per Regulation 3(4)), including exposure to incoming signals (e.g., API endpoints).

  4. For AWS/Azure: Leverage built-in tools like AWS Security Hub or Azure Security Center to automate risk identification.

  5. Reference: ISP042-Software Development Policy

  6. Secure design

  7. Design applications and systems to minimise attack surfaces, e.g., segment networks/functions to prevent a compromise in one part affecting others.

  8. Design applications and systems to be patched rapidly without the need for downtime.

  9. Ensure security-critical functions are protected and located appropriately (e.g., in isolated VPCs on AWS or Virtual Networks on Azure).

  10. Systems and application must not be publicly accessible unless there is a clear business justification.

  11. Test environments must only be accessible from authorise systems and/or IP addresses.

  12. Ensure PII is minimised and protected (e.g., anonymisation where possible).

  13. Do not use production data in test environments.

  14. Use AWS Well-Architected Framework Security Pillar and Azure Well-Architected Framework for design reviews.

  15. All systems must be recoverable, ensure that backups form part of all designs. ISP043-Information Backup Policy

  16. Align designs with OWASP Application Security Verification Standard (ASVS) levels, targeting Level 2 for standard applications and Level 3 for critical ones.

  17. Secure Coding and Implementation

  18. Follow secure coding standards from OWASP Top 10 and align with Code of Practice Section 3: Technical Guidance Measures (e.g., Management Plane 1 for access controls).

  19. Implement input validation to protect against injection attacks, especially for functions exposed to incoming signals.

  20. Use least privilege principles for access ISP013-Privileged Access Rights Policy

  21. For APIs: Enforce rate limiting, JWT tokens, and API gateways.

  22. Reference: ISP042-Software Development Policy

  23. For cloud environments, use infrastructure as code (IaC) tools like Terraform with security scanning (Aikido) to ensure secure configurations.

  24. Authentication and authorisation

We secure the confidentiality, integrity, and authenticity of communicating with clients and actions across transport and application layers.

Transport layer:

  • All communications must use HTTPS with TLS 1.3 or higher.

  • For AWS/Azure: Enable TLS termination at load balancers (e.g., AWS ALB, Azure Application Gateway) and enforce HSTS.

Application layer:

  • Users authenticate via:

  • Username/password plus TOTP (if enabled) for multi-factor authentication (MFA).

  • SAML SSO via trusted identity providers (e.g., Azure Entra ID).

  • On success, issue session tokens (e.g., JWT) with short expiry (configurable, default 30 minutes).

  • Implement role-based access control (RBAC) and attribute-based access control (ABAC) where appropriate to enforce fine-grained authorizations

  • Encryption

  • Encrypt all sensitive data in transit and at rest.

  • Use AWS KMS or Azure Key Vault for secrets management.

  • Personally Identifiable Information must always be encrypted over untrusted networks; use AES-256 or equivalent.

  • Rotate encryption keys regularly and manage secrets securely, avoiding hard coding in applications.

  • Monitoring and logging

  • Integrate logging for all critical events (e.g., authentication failures, access to sensitive data).

  • Use AWS CloudWatch/GuardDuty or Azure Monitor/Sentinel for real-time monitoring and anomaly detection.

  • Retain logs for at least 13 months (per Code of Practice Section 5).

  • Alert on suspicious activity, e.g., via email/SMS to security team.

  • Testing and vulnerability management

  • Conduct open-source dependency, static/dynamic application and secrets security testing using Aikido.

  • Perform penetration testing annually or on major changes.

  • For AWS/Azure: Use Security Hub or Defender for automated scans.

  • Patch vulnerabilities promptly, prioritising critical findings within 14 days. ISP036-Management of technical vulnerabilities

  • Reference: ISP042-Software Development Policy Section "Security testing in development and acceptance."

  • Secure business logic

  • Design and implement business logic to prevent abuse, such as excessive usage, workflow bypassing, or unauthorised state transitions (i.e. user to admin), as highlighted in OWASP Business Logic Abuse Top 10.

  • Test for business logic flaws including data validation, ability to forge requests, integrity checks, process timing, number of records returned, ability to bypass steps, and abuse of functionality.

  • Model business processes to identify and mitigate flaws that could lead to unintended behaviour.

  • Error handling and input/output sanitisation

  • Applications and services must not leak sensitive information in error messages.

  • Sanitise all inputs and outputs to prevent attacks like XSS or injection.

  • Use structured exception handling and provide generic error messages to users while logging detailed errors internally.

  • Third-party and supply chain security

  • Assess third-party libraries and services for vulnerabilities using Aikido.

  • Maintain a software bill of materials (SBOM) for all applications.

  • Ensure right-of-use and licensing requirements are met.

  • Secure deployment and operations

  • Use secure CI/CD pipelines with automated security gates.

  • Implement blue-green deployments or canary releases to minimise downtime during updates.

  • For containerised apps scan images for vulnerabilities and enforce runtime security.

docs.title: Document Objective
docs.text:
This Physical Security Standard provides detailed requirements for physical security controls at Community Fibre to prevent unauthorised access, damage, or interference with information assets and infrastructure. It supports the ISMS by detailing controls from ISO/IEC 27001:2022 Annexe A.7, and the NCSC Cyber Assessment Framework Principle B2 aligns with regulatory requirements, including the Telecommunications (Security) Act 2021.

This document meets the following clauses:

  • Information Security Management System ISO/IEC 27001:2022 -- A.7: Physical controls

  • NCSC Cyber Assessment Framework (CAF) v3.1 - Principle B2

  • The Electronic Communications (Security Measures) Regulations 2022 Reg 3(3)(a) Protect network from external threats (including physical); Code of Practice sections on site protection, access, monitoring, and environmental resilience

docs.title: Scope and principles
docs.text:
This standard applies to all in-scope physical locations and assets, personnel, and contractors at Community Fibre, including offices, data centres, and exchanges. It covers the lifecycle of physical assets and integrates with logical security measures.

Key principles, informed by ISO 27001 and NCSC Cyber Assessment Framework:

  • Establish perimeters and monitoring to prevent and detect unauthorised access.

  • Controls proportionate to asset sensitivity (per ISP037) and risks (e.g., exposed edge equipment).

  • Protect against environmental threats and ensure continuity.

  • Physical security supports logical controls (e.g., no physical access bypassing authentication).

Physical security is managed by Network Technology, Network Operations, Security Operations, and IT, with oversight from the ISMS Board.

docs.title: # Purpose
docs.text:
To prevent unauthorised physical access, damage and interference to the organisation's information and other associated assets. [1]

  • Areas to consider for physical security include:

  • Head office

  • Data centres

  • Exchanges

  • Remote working locations

  • Define security perimeters, including their locations and strengths, based on security requirements for the assets inside the area.

  • For sites where network equipment is located, physically and logically separate vulnerable equipment (exposed edge, e.g., CPE, OLT, roadside cabinets) from security-critical functions; no sensitive data stored in exposed edges.

  • Any sensitive equipment that is within the public domain will have all CFL branding removed from the public view, and instead use unique identifiers

  • Ensure physically secure perimeters for buildings or sites with sensitive processing facilities, eliminating gaps or easy break-in areas. Employ robust construction materials for exterior roofs, walls, ceilings, and floors.

  • Secure external doors from unauthorised access using mechanisms such as bars, alarms, and locks.

  • Ensure that doors and windows are securely locked when unattended. Additionally, consider implementing external protective measures for windows, particularly those on the ground floor, as well as for ventilation points.

  • Ensure that fire doors are equipped with alarms, monitored, and routinely tested within security perimeters, including walls, to meet the required resistance standards. Additionally, ensure that failsafe operation protocols are strictly adhered to.

  • Conduct perimeter inspections and testing at least annually to confirm integrity.

  • Conduct monthly spot-checks.

docs.title: # Purpose
docs.text: To ensure that only authorised physical access to the organisation's information and other associated assets occurs. [1]

docs.title: # General
docs.text:
For the areas where we must consider physical security, refer to A.7.1: Physical security perimeter.

Our main office is within a serviced office facility. Therefore, many of the requirements for Physical entry controls are the responsibility of the landlord as one of our service suppliers. Our assurance for physical entry is managed through the controls relating to Supplier relationships: A.5.19, A.5.20, A.5.21 and A.5.22

  • Unless monitored by reception staff during regular working hours, initial building access is controlled with a building access code, which is known only to the tenants in the building, building security and facilities management staff.

  • Key parts of the building, including where our offices are based, are only accessible via perimeter pass or individual identifiable code provided to members of staff to be able to access appropriate areas of the building for the specified role, responsibility and requirement to conduct their role

  • All cleaners and security guards around the building are vetted and managed by the supplier. Cleaning within our office is carried out by building service staff.

docs.title: # Visitors
docs.text:
A reception area, constituting part of the serviced office facility, is operational during standard working hours and serves to receive guests and oversee their entry and exit.

  • Visitor logs are held by reception staff.

  • Staff issued with perimeter passes must always carry them whilst in the building.

  • All visitors are supervised within our offices.

docs.title: # Delivery and loading areas and incoming material
docs.text:
The delivery and loading area is under the responsibility of the supplier of the serviced office facility. However, upon assessment of this area, we have observed the following:

The delivery and loading area is located at the rear of the building and is regulated as follows:

  • The internal and external doors must be secured and kept locked at all times when not in use.

  • When the external doors are open, the internal doors must be kept securely locked, and vice versa.

  • CCTV cameras are installed both externally and internally.

docs.title: # Sensitive processing areas
docs.text:
Data centres and exchange facilities are sites that house security-critical infrastructure and possess distinct threat profiles associated with increased risks compared to other areas, such as our headquarters. Access to these locations, therefore:

  • Access is restricted solely to authorised personnel. There exists a procedure for the provisioning, review, updating, and revocation of access rights.

  • Securely maintain a comprehensive audit trail of all access and authentication information.

  • Have a process and technical mechanisms for access management. (e.g., key exchange, key audit)

  • Authentication can include access cards, biometrics or multi-factor authentication, such as an access card and PIN.

  • Physical security must be overseen by on-site security personnel.

  • Personal belongings must be inspected upon entry and exit.

  • Require visible identification to be worn; unaccompanied visitors with no visible identification must be reported to security personnel.

  • Supplier personnel must only be granted temporary access, which must be authorised and monitored.

  • Lower risk tolerance should be maintained in multi-tenanted sites.

  • A key management process must be maintained to manage physical keys or codes. An annual key audit must be completed.

docs.title: # Purpose
docs.text: To prevent unauthorised physical access, damage and interference to the organisation's information and other associated assets in offices, rooms and facilities. [1]

docs.title: # Sensitive processing areas
docs.text:
• Shared sites such as data centres and exchanges must employ consistent security measures and maintain segregation from co-tenants.

  • Must not be easily identifiable by unauthorised persons.

  • Critical facilities should be located away from public access.

  • Buildings should be non-descript; directory listing must not disclose sensitive processing or security-critical areas.

  • Alarm codes are to be changed immediately, and PIN codes invalidated when employees depart from the organisation, in accordance with the exit and change procedures outlined in section A.5.18: Access rights.

  • We adhere to standard health and safety protocols as recommended by the facilities providers (offices or data centres).

docs.title: # Office
docs.text:
• Perimeter passes must only allow tenants into the relevant and authorised parts of the building.

  • Shared private meeting facilities are available for use by staff and visitors. The supplier manages these facilities, and all staff members are responsible for ensuring that any personal or organisational assets, as well as other information, are removed before vacating the room.

  • If a shared meeting room is used over multiple days, then, if appropriate, materials can be left overnight so long as;

  • The room is locked and secured

  • It is agreed with the facilities supplier that no cleaning or other room changes take place (if sensitive materials are in place); and

  • the material is obscured from view by other tenants, e.g. placing blinds over the windows looking into the hallway.

docs.title: # Purpose
docs.text: To detect and deter unauthorised physical access. [1]

docs.title: # Sensitive processing areas
docs.text:
• Physical premises should be monitored by surveillance systems, which can include guards, alarms, CCTV and physical security information management software either managed internally or by a monitoring service provider.

  • Access to buildings that house critical systems should be continuously monitored to detect unauthorised access or suspicious behaviour (e.g., CCTV, intrusion detection systems) in sensitive processing areas, with logs or records retained for at least 13 months.

  • Motion sensors and contact alarm triggers must be installed to applicable standards and periodically tested.

  • Alarms should cover all external doors and accessible windows. Unoccupied areas should always be alarmed.

docs.title: # Office
docs.text:
• Our principal office is located within a serviced office facility; consequently, the landlord assumes responsibility for many of the requirements pertaining to physical security monitoring.

  • Our assurance for Physical security monitoring is managed through the controls relating to Supplier relationships: A.5.19, A.5.20, A.5.21 and A.5.22.

docs.title: Protecting against physical and environmental threats (A.7.5)
# Purpose
docs.text: To prevent or reduce the consequences of events originating from physical and environmental threats. [1]

docs.title: # Sensitive processing areas
docs.text:
• Risk assessments must be conducted to identify the potential consequences of physical and environmental threats before beginning critical operations.

  • Consider risks arising from physical and environmental threats, including fire, flooding, earthquakes, explosions, civil unrest, toxic waste, emissions, and other natural or human-made disasters. Seek specialised consultation on effective management strategies for these concerns.

  • Locate and construct physical premises considering local topography (e.g., elevation, bodies of water, fault lines) and urban threats (e.g., high-profile areas for unrest, crime, or terrorism).

  • Fire suppression systems must be able to detect and send alarms or contain fire damage at an early stage.

  • Flood detection systems must be able to detect and send alarms or contain flood damage at an early stage and not damage essential IT infrastructure or key systems.

  • Suppression systems should not harm essential CFL IT and Infrastructure systems.

  • Regular maintenance/servicing must be conducted within the recommended manufacturers \' guidelines

  • Systems must be installed to protect both server and client information systems against electrical surges or similar events to minimise the consequences of such events.

docs.title: # Office
docs.text: • The provider of serviced offices bears the obligation to safeguard the buildings from external and environmental hazards. This encompasses the installation of fire extinguishers and related control measures in accordance with established standards. Our assurance of protection against these risks is governed by the controls related to Supplier relationships: A.5.19, A.5.20, A.5.21, and A.5.22

docs.title: # Purpose
docs.text: To protect information and other associated assets in secure areas from damage and unauthorised interference by personnel working in these areas. [1]

docs.title: # Sensitive processing areas
docs.text:
• Knowledge of activities and locations for areas containing security-critical infrastructure is disclosed on a need-to-know basis.

  • No work by third parties or contractors in areas containing security-critical infrastructure without supervision.

  • Photographs and video recordings in areas containing security-critical infrastructure may only be taken if authorised by Network Operations or Technology management.

  • Only approved end-user devices are permitted to enter and operate in areas containing security-critical infrastructure.

docs.title: # Office
docs.text:
• Our Head Office environment holds no security-critical services, and our assets are hosted within secure datacentre and in specific cloud locations; no area has been determined as a sensitive processing area.

  • Breakout or meeting rooms must be used in planning or other sensitive customer work, engaging people on a 'need-to-know' basis to avoid risk of information leakage into the main open-plan office, where it is not required to be shared.

  • Staff who work on security-critical services will do so using privileged access workstations in an area of the office that prevents other staff from seeing their work or will perform this work from home (e.g. Network engineers).

  • Currently, there is no need to display emergency procedures above and beyond the standard fire and emergency exit notices provided by the landlord of the serviced office building where our office is located.

  • Staff and others using our offices are reminded of the need to avoid leaving "Confidential" or "Strictly Confidential" materials where others might see them (e.g. through use of simple messages by the room exit and staff training). Secure working is further reinforced via our policy for Remote Working.

docs.title: # Purpose
docs.text:
To reduce the risks of unauthorised access, loss, and damage to information on desks, screens and in other accessible locations during and outside regular working hours. [1]

  • "Strictly confidential" information must not be left alone or exposed to unauthorised users at any point.

  • "Confidential" information on paper or electronic storage media, must be secured when not needed, especially when the office is vacated (ideally in paperless form in the first instance, otherwise locked in the desk pedestal, filing cabinet or other furniture at home or in the office)

  • Incoming and outgoing mail points are monitored by facilities management staff.

  • Documents containing "Confidential", or "Strictly confidential" information must be removed from printers immediately.

  • Devices must have a lock screen enabled.

  • There is no need to physically secure devices if the room in which the device is held has adequate security (e.g., door locks, or it is within trusted premises)

  • If there is any concern for safety, then employees must take their device with them.

  • Care must be taken to protect Confidential or Strictly Confidential when in public areas as data may be disclosed inadvertently or intentionally. Be careful where you take a call that covers sensitive information and try to position yourself in a busy area so that your device screen cannot be seen, or you cannot be overheard..

docs.title: # Purpose
docs.text:
To mitigate risks associated with physical and environmental threats, as well as unauthorised access and damage.

  • Site equipment to minimise unnecessary access to work areas and prevent unauthorised entry. (e.g., away from windows, elevated for flood protection).

  • Position sensitive data-processing facilities to minimise the risk of unauthorised viewing during operation.

  • Implement controls to reduce physical and environmental risks (e.g., theft, fire, explosives, smoke, water/supply failure, dust, vibration, chemicals, electrical/communications interference, electromagnetic radiation, vandalism).

  • Clear, established rules for eating, drinking, and smoking near information processing facilities.

  • Monitor environmental conditions such as temperature and humidity that could impact facility operations.

  • Install lightning protection on all buildings and install filters on incoming power and communication lines.

  • Use specialised protections (e.g., keyboard membranes) for equipment in industrial settings.

  • Protect equipment containing confidential information from risks of electromagnetic leakage.

  • Physically segregate organisation-managed facilities from external ones.

docs.title: # Purpose
docs.text:
To prevent loss, damage, theft or compromise of off-site devices and interruption to the organisation's operations. [1]

  • Avoid leaving equipment and storage media unattended in public or unsecured places.

  • Manage storage media lifecycle: Inventory, secure transport, and encryption for sensitive data.

  • Prohibit unauthorised removal; use approved media for transfers.

  • Follow manufacturers\' instructions for protection (e.g., against electromagnetic fields, water, heat, humidity, dust).

  • When transferring off-premises equipment between individuals or parties, keep a chain-of-custody log with responsible names and organisations. Securely delete unnecessary information before the transfer.

  • Require authorisation before removing equipment and media from premises; record all removals for audit trails (see 5.14).

  • Protect against unauthorised viewing (for example, on public transport) and shoulder surfing.

  • Activate location tracking and remote data wiping.

For permanently installed equipment outside premises (e.g., Exchanges, roadside cabinets), which face higher risks of damage, theft, or eavesdropping, consider location-specific measures including:

  • Physical security monitoring (see 7.4)

  • Protection against physical and environmental threats (see 7.5)

  • Physical access and tamper-proofing controls (e.g., secure boot)

  • Logical access controls.

docs.title: # Purpose
docs.text:
To ensure that only authorised disclosure, modification, removal, or destruction of information on storage media is permitted. [1]

Consider these guidelines for managing removable storage media.

  • Establish and communicate a policy specific to removable storage media to users and handlers.

  • Require authorisation before removing storage media from the organisation and record removals for audit purposes.

  • Store media in a safe, secure environment according to information classification, protecting against environmental threats (e.g., heat, moisture, humidity, electronic fields, ageing) following manufacturers\' specifications.

  • Use cryptographic techniques to protect sensitive or integrity-critical data on removable media.

  • Transfer information to new media before degradation renders it unreadable.

  • Store multiple copies of valuable information on separate media to minimise the risk of damage or loss.

  • Register removable media to minimise information loss risks.

  • Enable removable media ports (e.g., SD card slots, USB ports) only if organisationally necessary.

  • Monitor information transfers to removable media when used.

  • Information risks unauthorised access, misuse, or corruption during physical transport (e.g., via post or courier).

Note: Media includes paper documents. Apply security measures from 5.14 for physical transfers.

Refer to ISP044-Secure Disposal Policy for secure disposal and destruction of media containing data.

docs.title: # Purpose
docs.text:
To prevent loss, damage or compromise of information and other associated assets, or interruption to the organisation's operations due to failure and disruption of supporting utilities. [1]

  • Configure, operate, and maintain utility-supporting equipment in accordance with the manufacturers\' specifications.

  • Regularly evaluate utilities to ensure they can support business growth and coordinate effectively with other utilities.

  • Regularly check and test utility-supporting equipment to ensure it functions correctly.

  • If necessary, implement alarms to detect utility malfunctions.

  • If required, supply utilities with multiple feeds and varied physical routing.

  • If connected to a network, keep utility-supporting equipment on a separate network from information processing facilities.

  • Connect utility-supporting equipment to the internet only when necessary and secure it.

  • Provide emergency lighting and communication systems. Locate emergency switches and valves for power, water, gas, or other utilities near emergency exits or equipment rooms.

  • Record and provide emergency contact details for outages.

Other information: Enhance network connectivity redundancy by establishing multiple routes from various utility providers.

docs.title: # Purpose
docs.text:
To prevent loss, damage, theft, or compromise of information and other associated assets, and to prevent interruptions to the organisation's operations related to power and communications cabling. [1]

  • Install power and telecommunications lines underground within information processing facilities where feasible, or use suitable alternative protections (e.g., floor cable protectors, utility poles). For underground cables, safeguard against accidental cuts (e.g., armoured conduits, presence signals).

  • Keep power cables separate from communications cables to avoid interference.

  • For sensitive or critical systems, consider implementing supplementary controls:

  • Install armoured conduits, locked rooms or boxes, and alarms at inspection or termination points.

  • Use electromagnetic shielding for cables.

  • Perform regular technical checks and physical inspections to identify unauthorised attached devices.

  • Manage access to patch panels and cable rooms (e.g., mechanical keys, PINs).

  • Utilise fibre-optic cables.

  • Clear and recognisable cable labels at each end with source and destination details for physical identification and inspection.

  • Consult a specialist for advice on managing risks from cabling incidents or malfunctions.

  • Conduct tampering checks when visiting areas that are accessible to the public, and random checks on other locations annually. Report and record any s

Other information: Power and telecommunications cabling may be shared among multiple organisations in co-located premises.

docs.title: # Purpose
docs.text:
To prevent loss, damage, theft or compromise of information and other associated assets and interruption to the organisation's operations caused by lack of maintenance. [1]

  • Maintain equipment according to the supplier\'s recommended service intervals and specifications.

  • Establish and oversee an organisational maintenance programme.

  • Allow only authorised personnel to carry out repairs and maintenance.

  • Record all suspected or actual faults and preventive or corrective maintenance.

  • Implement suitable controls for scheduled maintenance, taking into account whether on-site or external personnel are involved; ensure maintenance staff sign confidentiality agreements.

  • Supervise on-site maintenance personnel.

  • Authorise and oversee remote maintenance access.

  • Implement off-premises asset security measures (see 7.9) if information-containing equipment is taken for maintenance.

  • Adhere to insurance-mandated maintenance obligations.

  • Inspect equipment post-maintenance for tampering and proper function before reactivation.

  • Use secure disposal or reuse measures (see 7.14) when equipment is to be disposed of.

Other information: Equipment encompasses information processing facility components, UPS and batteries, power generators, alternators, converters, and physical intrusion systems.

docs.title: Secure disposal or re-use of equipment (A.7.14)
# Purpose
docs.text:
To prevent leakage of information from equipment to be disposed of or reused. [1]

  • Check equipment for stored media before disposal or reuse.

  • Physically destroy storage media containing confidential or copyrighted information or delete/overwrite data using irreversible methods, not standard deletion. Refer to 7.10 for secure disposal and contact Security Operations for guidance on deletion.

  • Remove labels or markings that identify organisation, classification, owner, system, or network before disposal, including resale or donation.

  • Consider removing security controls (e.g., access controls, surveillance equipment) at lease end or move-out, depending on:

  • Lease requirement to restore to original condition

  • Risks of leaving sensitive data (e.g., user lists, videos/images) for the next tenant

  • Reuse potential at new facility.

Other information: For damaged equipment with storage media, perform a risk assessment to determine physical destruction vs. repair/discard. Careless disposal/reuse can compromise information.

Please refer to the ISP044-Secure Disposal Policy.pdf for guidance.

docs.title: Regulatory requirements
docs.text:
• Physical security measures protect against external threats (Reg 3), including site perimeters, access restrictions, and monitoring.

  • For shared/third-party sites: Ensure equivalent security (CoP Chap 6).

  • Testing: Include physical access simulations in penetration tests (CoP Chap 13).

  • Resilience: Address environmental/geopolitical threats in continuity planning (CoP Para 2.95).

docs.title: Monitoring and review
docs.text:
• Conduct annual audits and risk assessments, review after incidents or changes.

  • Integrate physical security incidents into ISMS reporting.

docs.title: Responsibilities
docs.text:
• Network Operations and Network Technology: Implement and maintain controls.

  • Security Operations: Monitor and respond to incidents.

  • All Staff: Report issues; comply with access rules.

  • ISMS Board: Oversight and approval.

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text:
The purpose of this document is to provide an overview of Community Fibre Limited, the activities it conducts and the ISMS standards of operation it conforms to.

Community Fibre Limited handles staff, vendor, corporate, customer and customer personnel data and the business must be able to demonstrate that information security has been integrated into processes, and that all information is managed securely.

Certification to ISO 27001:2022 of the Community Fibre Limited ISMS will provide assurance internally to management and stakeholders, as well as to customer and other interested parties, that its information is managed in a controlled and secure manner, and that Community Fibre Limited is committed to providing a reliable level of service.

The company is committed to meeting regulatory and compliance obligations, including the UK GDPR/Data Protection Act 2018 and the Telecommunications (Security) Act 2021. Compliance with these regulations ensures that Community Fibre maintains high standards of assurance, resilience, and accountability.

The ISMS is designed to align with ISO 27001:2022 and any standard adopting the Annex SL structure.

docs.title: Overview of the organisation
docs.text:
Founded in 2010, Community Fibre provides high-speed broadband across Greater London and Surrey through its fully owned and operated optical fibre network.

The company is committed to serving multi and single-dwelling, businesses and increasingly wholesale partners. Community Fibre offers competitive pricing, exceptional customer support, and high-speed, reliable, full-fibre connectivity. Its dedication to customer service has earned it one of the highest Trustpilot ratings among UK ISPs.

Community Fibre provides:

  • Fibre broadband services to residential and business customers.

  • Fibre network wholesale services to other and often larger UK telecoms businesses.

  • Support and billing services for residential and business customers.

docs.title: Purposes
docs.text:
The purpose of the ISMS and information security program is to protect the organisation, network and business infrastructure, and the staff and customer information it collects, processes, and stores.

This is achieved through the documented policies and procedures, education and awareness initiatives, and appropriate and proportionate technical and organisational controls. The scope of the ISMS encompasses core network services and business systems and operations.

Community Fibre recognises the critical value and importance of securing the information and network assets that drive our business. The ISMS supports our key strategic aims of:

Excellent service -- Security continuity (the practice of keeping Community Fibre's data and systems protected and operational, no matter what disruptions hit us) differentiates our services from other organisations, exceeds customer expectations, and enables us to operate effectively in an increasingly regulated environment.

Network and information asset protection -- Through this ISMS, we aim to minimise risks associated with malicious activities, accidental damage, or disruptions to information assets and network infrastructure, regardless of their form (digital, physical, or otherwise).

Regulatory and contractual requirements - Drives compliance with relevant statutory regulations, including the Telecommunications (Security) Act 2021 and UK GDPR/Data Protection Act 2018, as well as contractual requirements.

docs.title: Determining the scope of the information security management system
docs.text:
The scope of the ISMS is defined as

Community Fibre Limited operating within Greater London, providing broadband services to residential, business and wholesale customers; the core network infrastructure and UK customer data processing within its business software systems, supported by Customer Services, Network Technology, HR, Commercial, Finance, Marketing, Operations, Information Technology, Information Security and Data Protection.

Exclusions to the ISMS scope

The boundary of the ISMS Scope can be further identified by the exclusion of these specific activities:

  • The Community Fibre Limited lower tier exchanges, street cabinets, ducting, poles; training, testing and equipment and hardware storage facilities.

  • The physical security of non-Community Fibre Limited locations (e.g., customer sites, private homes) is out of scope of the ISMS. However, other security measures applied to Community Fibre Limited Information Assets that are used in these locations (e.g., laptops, mobiles) remain within scope.

Detailed Scope description

The ISMS scope covers Community Fibre\'s secure data handling, core network infrastructure, and aggregation sites, aligning with regulatory requirements. The Statement of Applicability details selected controls for risk treatment, justifying inclusion of all 93 Annex A controls from ISO 27001:2022. Figure 1 summarises the scope and governance structure.

The ISMS objectives apply to all in-scope elements. There is mandatory compliance with the ISMS within this scope.

{width="6.406724628171479in" height="6.4806058617672795in"}

Figure 1.: Representation of the Community Fibre Services (yellow), Governance (green) and Processes (blue)

Zones

Community Fibre zones are numbered 1-7 in Figure 1 above.

Z.1 Applications -- Community Fibre business applications: TCS Hobs, Apigee, Amazon Connect, Omningage, Zinier, Domo, Mobile Applications, public website, ArcGIS.

Z.2 Data Services -- Third-party services (IaaS, PaaS) managed by Community Fibre such as AWS, Azure, Google Cloud, MongoDB and AWS RDS for the storage and processing of critical data and services such as Hobs, the public website, GIS systems and data.

Z.3 Vendors -- Fully and partially managed SaaS applications such as Zinier, Domo, Cloudflare, BambooHR, Microsoft (M365, Azure), AWS, Google, GitHub and Gitlab, and CCI, TCS, Cognizant, Cisco, Adtran, Juniper, Palo Alto.

Z.4 Data handling -- Data storage, data access, querying and reporting methods such as AWS RDS and API's include Google Apigee, Domo.

Z.5 Applications and Data Interfaces -- Methods for presenting and accessing services and data including code repositories, protocols, firewalls and webservices hosted in AWS, Azure and Cloudflare.

Z.6 Core Network and Technology -- Data centre locations, primary exchange locations, core hardware architecture, network management, automation, monitoring.

Z.7 Identity -- Identity providers, cloud-based, on-premises, privileged access management, joiners-movers-leavers, just-in-time, role-based access management, authorisation, audit, monitoring.

Infrastructure

In scope:

  1. Infrastructure in the Applications zone (Zone 1) includes:

a. Applications and containers running code that process Community Fibre Limited data.

b. Interfaces, such as web or reporting services for accessing, querying, or downloading data.

c. Source code

  1. Infrastructure in the Data Services zone (Zone 2), including database services, and the software and applications in each virtual compute instance.

  2. Infrastructure in the Vendors zone (Zone 3) including authentication configuration and company data stored and transferred in or out each SaaS service.

  3. Infrastructure in the Data handling zone (Zone 4) includes cloud data storage, cloud-based query logic such as APIs, and including the any endpoint devices that store company data, and any other services that store company data.

  4. Infrastructure in Data handling zone (Zone 5), used to securely deliver data or services.

  5. Infrastructure in the Core network and technology zone (Zone 6), used to deliver and manage broadband services to customer premises.

  6. Infrastructure in the Identity zone (Zone 7), used to authenticate and authorise users, vendors and customers and grant access to approved data and services when required.

The above zones will be referred to in all ISMS documentation as the "Community Fibre infrastructure".

Out of scope:

  1. Customer premises.

  2. Lower tier exchanges and hardware, street cabinets and hardware, ducting, poles.

  3. Training, equipment and hardware storage facilities such as Longwood. Network equipment stored at Longwood are configured at point of deployment and restored to factory default or wiped before returned to Longwood.

People

In scope:

  1. All staff members directly employed by Community Fibre Limited.

  2. All contractors or staff (including BPO type services) employed by service providers that have access to Community Fibre infrastructure for example CCI South Africa, TCS, Cognizant and Orange Moldova.

  3. IT and support staff and contractors working on the Community Fibre in-scope infrastructure. Contracts, service, and operating level agreements must accord with the ISMS.

  4. Suppliers and data providers who enter a contractual agreement with Community Fibre Limited.

Out of scope:

Users, support staff and data providers while they are not interacting with Community Fibre infrastructure or data.

Services

In scope:

Services delivered on Community Fibre infrastructure can be summarised as data capture, process, access, and storage services, including:

  1. Data captured, processed, and stored through the public company website.

  2. All data acquisition activities involving external third parties.

  3. All data enrichment activities involving external third parties.

  4. All transfers of data to and from external third parties.

  5. All internal software development activities.

docs.title: Information security management system
docs.text:
Community Fibre Limited has established, implemented, maintained, and will continually improve an information security management system in accordance with ISO27001. This ISMS provides information as to how we meet these requirements, with reference to key processes and policies, as appropriate.

docs.title: Leadership
