docs.title: Introduction
docs.text: AI Use Principles and Values apply to all Employees on the use or implementation of AI within Community Fibre, including the use of Large Language Models (LLM), Generic AI, Generative AI, etc. The design principles from chapter "4. AI System Onboarding Requirements" also applies when designing or implementing an AI system.

docs.title: Roles & Responsibilities
docs.text: A detailed overview of specific actions, along with the designated owners for each action, is available in Section 5.7, titled \"Overview of All Actions with Owners.\"

docs.title: Be open and transparent about the use of AI
docs.text: Employees must be open and transparent about the use of AI tools within their departments and teams. This includes sharing the purpose of the tool, how it is being utilised, and the potential impact on processes or decision-making.

docs.title: Do not use personal data or confidential information
docs.text:
It is strictly prohibited to use personal data as defined in the Community Fibre Data Protection Policy, such as telephone numbers, call detail records, email-addresses or financial information, for AI applications without a proper legal ground and security & data protection measures. Confidential business data with a competitive advantage must also be carefully protected.

An AI Risk Assessment must be performed in case you need to process personal data and/or confidential information with an AI tool.

docs.title: Use AI within your Expertise
docs.text: Use AI tools only within your own domain of knowledge or expertise. This means you should understand the output of the AI and be able to verify it.

docs.title: Guard Against Bias and Discrimination
docs.text: You must be aware of potential bias in AI systems, especially when these systems make decisions regarding customer interactions. You should take care to avoid producing discriminatory results.

docs.title: Trust, but Verify
docs.text: Never solely rely on the outcome of AI tools. Always check the results of AI tools to ensure they remain accurate and relevant.

docs.title: Hold yourself accountable for AI use
docs.text: You are personally responsible for the proper use of AI tools and must report and rectify any errors or issues. You are responsible for the outcome as it was produced by yourself.

docs.title: Consider implications of AI use
docs.text: Always consider whether the use of AI tools is responsible, especially when it affects customers.

docs.title: Be Aware of the AI Tool and its Related Risks
docs.text: As a user of AI tools, you must be fully aware of the capabilities, limitations, and potential risks associated with the use of these tools. This principle emphasises the importance of understanding AI systems to make informed and responsible decisions.

docs.title: Mandatory AI Risk Assessment
docs.text: If you intend to integrate an AI system into Community Fibre network or process confidential information (see ISP037-Information Classification and Handling Policy) or personal data within an AI system, a prior AI Risk Assessment is mandatory. This assessment is essential to proactively address compliance, privacy and security risks associated with the AI system\'s deployment and data handling practices.

docs.title: Report issues or concerns
docs.text: If you notice or experience any issues regarding AI system performance or ethical implications, report this immediately to dpo@communityfibre.co.uk.

docs.title: Progressive Implementation of AI Tools
docs.text: When AI functionalities are progressively integrated into existing software (e.g., Office 365, Adobe), these also need to be assessed. The integration should pass through an AI Risk Assessment process to ensure compliance with Community Fibre policies, even if the software is Community Fibre IT-provided. This ensures that any new AI capabilities, such as Microsoft Copilot, do not inadvertently expose personal or confidential information.

docs.title: Design & Implementation of AI tools: Requirements
Introduction
docs.text:
This chapter outlines the critical design requirements for ensuring the trustworthiness of AI systems within Community Fibre. It underscores the need to address a multitude of criteria valued by stakeholders. It highlights key characteristics, including validity, reliability, safety, security, accountability, transparency, explainability, interpretability, privacy enhancement and fairness with bias management.

These requirements must be carefully balanced within the specific context of AI system deployment to mitigate negative consequences effectively. [ref. 21]

docs.title: Roles & Responsibilities
docs.text: A detailed overview of specific actions, along with the designated owners for each action, is available in Section 5.7, titled \"Overview of All Actions with Owners.\"

docs.title: Valid and Reliable
docs.text: AI systems must be validated for their specific intended use, ensuring accuracy and reliability. Ongoing testing and monitoring are required to confirm systems perform as intended.

docs.title: Safe
docs.text: AI systems should be designed, developed, and deployed to avoid endangering human life, health, property, or the environment.

docs.title: Secure and Resilient
docs.text:
AI systems must be secure against unauthorised access and use, maintaining confidentiality, integrity, and availability. Refer to Community Fibre ISP001-ISMS Mandatory Clauses for applicable security policies, standards and guidelines.

Systems should be resilient, able to withstand and recover from adverse events and changes in their environment.

docs.title: Accountable and Transparent
docs.text:
AI systems must have clear accountability mechanisms, e.g. ensuring that operations, decisions, and methodologies of AI systems are understandable and traceable.

Transparency in AI operations, including decision-making processes, should be maintained, and documented.

docs.title: Explainable and Interpretable
docs.text:
AI systems should be explainable, with explicit representation of their operational mechanisms. Generic AI might have some limitations in terms of providing assurance of privacy and security such as general accuracy, lack of depth, lack of QA, resource intensive, lack of explainability (model design and operation may be difficult to explain).

When the use of an AI system has a legally binding effect on a data subject, or similarly significantly affects them, they must be given meaningful information about the logic of the AI system involved. Additional requirements from the Community Fibre Data Protection Policy apply.

docs.title: Privacy-Enhanced (if personal data will be processed)
docs.text: AI systems should adhere to the Community Fibre Data Protection Policy protecting user autonomy and data. A data privacy impact assessment should be performed to guide AI system design to enhance privacy, including using privacy-enhancing technologies (. e.g., anonymisation and encryption).

docs.title: Fair -- with Harmful Bias Managed
docs.text:
AI systems must be designed and operated to manage and mitigate harmful biases.

The AI system treats everyone equally, no matter their background or what group they belong to. This means the system should not make decisions that unfairly favour one group over another or discriminate based on things like a person\'s race, gender, age, or any other personal characteristic.

docs.title: Compliant Design
docs.text: AI Systems must be frequently reviewed using the assessments referred to in 4.4, to ensure it stays compliant with applicable laws and regulations, e.g. the EU AI Act and the DPA 2018/EU GDPR.

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text: When introducing a new AI system at Community Fibre, it\'s essential to fully understand its role, the risks involved, and its purpose. To ensure smooth integration, Community Fibre has established specific onboarding requirements. These requirements are designed to identify and address the risks and actions associated with each AI tool based on its unique features and intended use. This approach helps us integrate AI systems effectively and responsibly, ensuring they align with our organisational goals and standards.

docs.title: Roles & Responsibilities
docs.text: A detailed overview of specific actions, along with the designated owners for each action, is available in Section 5.7, titled \"Overview of All Actions with Owners.\"

docs.title: AI tools in existing systems
docs.text: When AI functionalities are progressively integrated into existing software (e.g., Office 365, Adobe), these also need to be assessed. The integration should pass through an AI Risk Assessment process to ensure compliance with Community Fibre policies, even if the software is Community Fibre IT-provided. This ensures that any new AI capabilities, such as Microsoft Copilot, do not inadvertently expose personal or confidential information.

docs.title: AI systems for one-off or testing purposes
docs.text: When using AI tools [ref. 13, 15, 16] for singular tasks or testing purposes the data shall remain within a secure and controlled environment; this shall be enforced contractually and with technical controls that can be demonstrated, and the AI System Registration and Intake Process shall be completed as part of project initiation or before one-off use.

docs.title: Integrated AI Functionalities
docs.text: New AI features in existing software shall be evaluated for potential risks, especially regarding data privacy and security. Employees must be trained on the use of AI functionalities and made aware of risks to privacy and security.

docs.title: AI System Registration and Intake Process
docs.text:
Every integrated AI system and tool proposed or in use within Community Fibre shall be registered using the designated AI Intake Form. The purpose of the Intake Form is:

  • To collect essential information about the AI system, including its purpose, data usage, and technical specifications.

  • To conduct an initial evaluation of potential risks associated with the AI system, it can be decided, based on the initial assessment, that the AI system poses too high a risk for use in Community Fibre.

  • To decide whether a comprehensive Privacy Assessment and/or AI Risk Assessment is necessary based on the preliminary findings.

The intake for can be found here: AI System Intake - CFL IT Support Portal - Jira Service Management (atlassian.net)

The information gathered from the AI Intake Form will be used to maintain an up-to-date AI Register, which serves as a centralised record of all AI systems and tools used within Community Fibre.

docs.title: AI Register Maintenance
docs.text:
Governance, Risk & Compliance will be responsible for maintaining the AI Register. This role includes:

  • Keeping oversight to ensure that the AI Register accurately reflects all AI systems and tools in use and that they are compliant with Community Fibre's AI policies and relevant regulations.

  • Supporting AI project teams, IT, legal, and compliance departments to ensure complete and accurate information is captured in the AI Register.

  • Managing access to the AI Register, ensuring that relevant stakeholders have the necessary visibility while maintaining confidentiality and data security.

  • Technical Owners are responsible for initiating the AI intake process, providing essential information about the AI system, and ensuring the information remains current.

docs.title: An AI Risk Assessment should be conducted:
docs.text:
For any new AI system or major update to an existing system covering one or more below:

  • If the AI system has the potential to significantly impact individuals, business operations, or decision-making processes.

  • When the AI system processes or potentially processes confidential information or strictly confidential data. (ISP037-Information Classification and Handling Policy)

  • For AI systems that are complex or use novel technologies, where risks might not be fully understood.

On a regular basis for existing AI systems to reassess risks and account for changes or updates.

docs.title: A Privacy Impact Assessment (DPIA) should be conducted:
docs.text:
• Whenever an AI system collects, processes, stores, or transmits personal data.

  • When there are significant changes to how personal data is processed, which could affect user privacy.

  • To ensure compliance with data protection laws (UK DPA 2018/EU GDPR).

  • On a regular basis (at every 2 years) for existing AI systems to reassess privacy risks and account for changes or updates.

Assessments must be reviewed and updated, if needed, at least biannually or whenever the AI system undergoes significant changes. These assessments should be conducted to verify that the implemented measures remain adequate in relation to its security, privacy, and other relevant risks, as well as to proactively identify and mitigate evolving security threats.

docs.title: Documentation of controls
docs.text:
For every AI system, the following must be documented:

  • The outcomes of AI Risk Assessments, Privacy Assessments, and Security Impact Assessments.

  • All measures and controls implemented to mitigate identified risks, protect privacy, and ensure security.

Documentation must be updated:

  • Whenever a new assessment is conducted, or an existing assessment is updated.

  • Following the implementation of any new measures or controls, or significant adjustments to existing ones.

  • To reflect any changes in AI system design, operation, or use that could influence the effectiveness of existing controls.

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text:
This chapter outlines the roles and responsibilities regarding the design, development, implementation, and use of AI within Community Fibre. .

An overview of specific actions with specific actions owner can be found in 5.7 Overview of all actions with owners.

docs.title: Business Owner
docs.text:
• The respective management responsible for the procurement and initiating the implementation or use of an AI system will be deemed Business Owner.

  • The Business Owner has the following responsibilities:

  • Ensure that objectives for the AI system align with overall business goals.

  • Develop a strategic plan for AI implementation, including timelines and resource allocation.

  • The Business Owner is responsible for overseeing the overall compliance of the AI system with Community Fibre policies, laws, regulations, and industry standards, including the AI Policy and the Data Protection Policy.

  • This role involves ensuring strategic alignment and accountability, providing guidance and support to the Technical Owner, and securing the resources necessary for effective implementation and compliance.

  • Establish accountability for decisions made by the AI system.

docs.title: Technical Owner
docs.text:
• The Technical Owner responsible for the development, testing and deployment and maintenance of AI systems, will be deemed as responsible Technical Owner.

  • The Technical Owner has the following responsibilities:

  • Develop, test, and deploy AI models aligned with company objectives.

  • Ensure that AI design requirements are considered.

  • Monitor AI systems for performance and ethical compliance.

  • Manage data quality and ethical sourcing for AI models.

  • Adhere to internal AI ethical guidelines and best practices.

  • Identify and mitigate operational risks in AI systems.

  • Report AI performance and risks to management and stakeholders

docs.title: Governance, Risk & Compliance (GRC)
docs.text:
• GRC is the responsibility of the ISMS Board, chaired by the Head of Security

  • The Head of Security will be responsible for:

  • AI Register Maintenance and oversight of AI Intakes

  • Establish policies and guidelines for ethical AI usage.

  • Defining and monitoring of AI Controls.

  • Facilitate risk assessments focusing on ethical, legal, and operational aspects of AI.

  • Support compliance with external regulations and internal AI policies.

  • Provide guidance on AI risk management and ethical considerations.

  • Facilitate training on AI risk, ethics, and compliance.

  • Monitor AI systems and processes for compliance and effectiveness.

docs.title: Community Fibre Technical Architecture Team
docs.text:
Community Fibre's Architecture team consists of subject matter experts and collaborate and obtain functional and non-functional requirements from the business. The core team should at least be represented by experts in:

  • IT

  • Data Science

  • Mass market marketing

  • Data Protection

  • Compliance and ethics

  • Legal & Regulatory

Community Fibre's Architecture team has the following responsibilities:

  • Provide multidisciplinary insights on AI projects, bridging gaps between technical, legal, compliance, and business perspectives.

  • Review AI projects for ethical considerations, including data privacy, fairness, and transparency.

  • Assist in interpreting AI policies in the context of specific projects, ensuring compliance and alignment.

  • Support a cohesive approach to AI implementation and governance.

docs.title: End-Users of AI Systems
docs.text:
End-users of AI Systems have the following responsibilities:

  • Provide feedback on AI system usability and effectiveness.

  • Adhere to the Community Fibre AI Policy, guidelines and best practices for AI system usage.

  • Participate in training and awareness programs related to AI.

  • Report issues or concerns regarding AI system performance or ethical implications.

docs.title: Policy
docs.text:
The objective of this policy is to establish principles for the secure development, acquisition, integration, and maintenance of software, scripts, and automation tools.

All activities will incorporate security by design, with explicit consideration of impacts to confidentiality, integrity, availability, privacy, and network resilience. This aligns with the principle of building security \"in\" to systems from the outset, as per ISO/IEC 27002:2022 controls A.8.25--A.8.29 and supports regulatory requirements under the Electronic Communications (Security Measures) Regulations 2022 to reduce risks of security compromises in public electronic communications networks and services.

Security requirements analysis and specification must be proportionate to the risk level, size, and scope of the activity, with analysis conducted as early as feasible to balance security benefits against project delivery risks.

Key considerations:

  • Identifying the need for analysis and specifications based on risk assessments, including exposure to incoming signals, sensitive data (e.g., content of signals or data controlling security-critical functions), and security-critical functions (e.g., those with significant impact on network operation).

  • The timing of analysis - earlier the better from a security perspective, but may introduce more risk to project delivery, so both sides of the risk equation must be carefully assessed and weighed.

  • Security requirements for:

  • Identification, authentication, and authorisation controls, including prevention of unauthorised access or interference.

  • Logging, monitoring, and analysis, with protection for tools that enable such functions.

  • Data classification and segregation, ensuring protection of sensitive data.

  • Controls on information transfer, including encryption for signals and data in transit.

  • Audit trails for remediation and recovery preparedness

  • Network architecture design aims to minimise the risks associated with the propagation of compromises throughout the network.

  • Trust boundaries must be established and maintained:

    • between areas such as internal and external networks, customer networks, partner networks, the internet and international networks

    • our networks and third-party administrator networks, such as those owned by network equipment suppliers and MSPs

    • between our security critical functions and functions in the access network or exposed edge

    • between management networks and other networks, including internal networks.

  • Integration of business continuity and disaster recovery requirements, aligned with service criticality and SLAs, including the ability to operate without reliance on overseas persons, equipment, or data where risks are identified.

docs.title: Secure software design
docs.text:
Threat modelling is a core component of secure design, identifying risks to software, scripts, and network functions, and enabling proportionate controls. Designs must consider the business value of information and processes, potential impacts from inadequate controls, and regulatory duties to design networks that reduce security compromise risks. Guidance for Application Security by Design is available on Jira: Application Security By Design

  • Design and requirements specifications must be documented, reviewed, and approved, reflecting evaluated security risks.

  • Information security designs, requirements, and controls must address:

  • Protection of security-critical functions and sensitive data.

  • Location and exposure of equipment (e.g., minimising reliance on assets located overseas).

  • Segregation to prevent compromise propagation.

  • Business continuity/disaster recovery must be integrated, ensuring restoration aligns with criticality and SLAs.

  • For automation scripts, designs must include modelling of impacts on provisioning, management, and orchestration or security-critical components to avoid unauthorised interference or data exposure.

Development environments

Segregating software development, testing and production environments minimises the likelihood of faulty code in production environments and networks, aligning with duties to protect critical functions and maintain architecture that reduces compromise risks.

  • Development, testing (including UAT), and production environments must be logically segregated.

  • Separate environments are mandatory for development, UAT, testing, and production, unless explicitly approved by the CIO with documented justification.

  • Sensitive production data, including network signals or operational data, must not be utilised in non-production environments. When authorised by the CIO, such data must be anonymised entirely or pseudonymised. If anonymisation is impractical, appropriate security measures equivalent to production standards must be applied.

  • Changes to any environment must follow a documented change management process, including verification of no unauthorised access.

  • Network Operations scripts should be developed within isolated environments that accurately simulate the production environment, ensuring that live network components are not exposed.

  • Web application frameworks must be used to aid in the development of secure web applications. The Open Web Application Security Project (OWASP) provides comprehensive resources.

docs.title: Secure development practices
docs.text:
Secure engineering principles must be applied across all development activities, including scripts for automation.

  • Secure system engineering principles, including those from OWASP for web applications and telecom-specific standards where applicable, must be documented, maintained, and enforced.

  • All development staff must undergo role-specific training on secure practices, threat modelling, and regulatory requirements.

  • The development lifecycle must be documented, with security gates for approval at key stages (e.g., design, code, test).

  • Secure repositories (e.g., version-controlled with access controls) must store all code, scripts, and documentation, ensuring confidentiality and integrity.

  • Source code and scripts must have versioning, descriptions, and documentation; access must adhere to least privilege and separation of duties.

  • Security hardening guidelines must be implemented across all components, including third-party libraries.

  • Third-party packages must be sourced from approved, trusted vendors; modifications for production use require standards approval and vulnerability assessments.

  • Robust frameworks must be used (e.g., OWASP-compliant for applications; secure scripting practices for automation).

  • Supply chain risks must be assessed per the Code of Practice, including vendor security assessments and restrictions on high-risk suppliers.

docs.title: Security testing in development and acceptance
docs.text:
Testing must verify security requirements and reduce vulnerabilities before production deployment, integrating static/dynamic analysis and peer reviews. Release processes must be documented and enforced.

  • Pre-release verification must include peer approval, UAT, open-source dependency scanning, static code analysis and dynamic analysis.

  • Developer tools (e.g., IDEs) must enable real-time vulnerability detection and remediation.

  • Security requirements, including the protection of sensitive data and critical functions, must be explicitly tested.

  • Internet-facing software and network tools must undergo independent penetration testing before launch and regular vulnerability scanning thereafter.

  • Internal-facing software, scripts, and automation must undergo regular vulnerability scanning.

  • Security scans and checks should be integrated into CI/CD pipelines, automatically preventing deployment when vulnerabilities are found.

Reference: https://communityfibre.atlassian.net/wiki/x/AgAyQg (Application Security By Design)

docs.title: Software testing and release
docs.text: To prevent vulnerabilities in production, testing and release must align with the documented ISD007-Software Release Management procedure.

docs.title: Outsourced development
docs.text:
Outsourced activities must comply with vendor management and third-party risk processes.

  • Outsourced development arrangements will follow the vendor management process and be subject to the information security third party assessment process.

  • Outsourced developers will be made aware of this policy and the defined secure system engineering principles.

  • Outsourced developers are required to adhere to this policy and the defined secure system engineering principles.

docs.title: Adherence to policy
docs.text: Failure to comply with this policy may result in disciplinary procedures up to and including termination of employment or contract.

docs.title: General Information
docs.text: This backup policy is designed to ensure the protection and availability of critical data and essential functions for Community Fibre. It establishes guidelines and procedures for backing up data, storing backups securely, and restoring data in the event of loss or corruption. By implementing this policy, Community Fibre aims to minimise the risk of data loss, maintain business continuity, and safeguard sensitive information.

docs.title: This document meets the following clauses:
docs.text: • Information Security Management System BS EN ISO/IEC 27001:2022 -- A.8.13: Information backup

docs.title: Scope
docs.text: This policy applies to all employees, contractors, and third parties who have access to Community Fibre\'s data and information systems. It covers all data and essential functions deemed critical to the organisation\'s operations, including but not limited to core network functions, customer information, financial records, intellectual property, network configurations, operational logs, and data related to security critical functions. The policy applies to data stored on subscription model services (SaaS), cloud infrastructure (AWS, Azure), physical devices, servers, databases, workstations, routers, switches, management systems, and other information systems managed by IT, Network Technology and Network Operations teams.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text: The purpose of this backup policy is to safeguard Community Fibre\'s data against loss, corruption, or unauthorised access. By establishing clear procedures for data backup and restoration, this policy ensures that critical information is available and secure, supporting business continuity and compliance with relevant regulations.

docs.title: Data classification
docs.text:
Data is classified based on its importance to business operations and regulatory definitions:

  • Strictly confidential data: Essential for business operations and includes sensitive data as per regulations (e.g., data controlling security-critical functions, customer databases, financial records, intellectual property). Requires frequent backups.

  • Confidential data: Valuable but not critical (e.g., internal communications, project files,). Backed up less frequently.

  • Non-essential data: Easily recreated or not necessary for operations (e.g., temporary files). May not require regular backups.

docs.title: Backup Schedule
docs.text:
• Strictly confidential data (critical): Full backup daily, full backup monthly, full annual backup, with online and offline copies replaced with reasonable frequency appropriate to the risk.

  • Confidential data (important): Full backup daily, full backup monthly, full annual backup.

  • Public (non-essential data): Backed up as needed or upon request.

Note: Backup procedures may vary depending on the type of system or data being backed up. Specific procedures for different systems are detailed in AWS+Backup and Rubrik. Backups must include information necessary to maintain normal operation of the network/service.

docs.title: Backup Storage
docs.text:
Backups are stored in multiple locations to ensure redundancy, disaster recovery:

  • Cloud: For additional redundancy and accessibility, using a secure cloud storage provider. Cloud-based backup storage must be duplicated across availability zones.

  • On-Site: For quick access and restoration (e.g., local servers or storage devices).

  • Off-Site: For disaster recovery, stored in a secure, geographically separate location within the UK.

  • Offline Copies: Proportionate offline copies (not exposed to network signals) must be maintained for critical information to enable recovery without risk of further compromise.

Retention periods are determined by system and data criticality and recovery requirements.

  • AWS: Full backups are retained for 35 days.

  • M365: Full backups are retained for 30 days. Monthly backups are retained for 12 months. Annual backups are retained for 3 years.

All copies of information necessary for normal operation must be retained within the UK.

docs.title: Backup Testing
docs.text:
• Regular testing is conducted to ensure backups can be restored successfully, including verification of online and offline copies.

  • Testing is performed quarterly, and results are documented.

  • Any issues identified during testing must be addressed promptly to maintain backup integrity and resilience.

docs.title: Recovery point and time objectives
docs.text:
Recovery Point Objective (RPO) and Recovery Time Objective (RTO) are defined to ensure timely recovery from security compromises or disruptions, which requires preparation for remediation and recovery, including maintaining backups and procedures to replace damaged information without further risk.

RPO: The maximum acceptable data loss period, determined by backup frequency and system criticality.

  • Strictly confidential (critical) systems/data: RPO ≤ 24 hours (achieved through daily full backups for security critical functions).

  • Confidential (important) systems/data: RPO ≤ 24 hours (achieved through daily full backups).

  • Non-essential systems/data: RPO ≤ 24 hours (aligned with daily backups).

RTO: The maximum acceptable time to restore operations, based on assessed security risks and business impact.

  • Strictly confidential (critical) systems/data: RTO ≤ 2 hours

  • Confidential (important) systems/data: RTO ≤ 24 hours.

  • Non-essential systems/data: RTO ≤ 48 hours.

These objectives must be reviewed annually or following risk assessments and prioritised accordingly. Procedures must ensure no further security compromise during recovery, using offline copies where proportionate.

docs.title: Security
docs.text:
• All backups must be encrypted both in transit and at rest using industry-standard encryption methods.

  • Immutable backups must be used for data which is critical to business operations. Immutability is defined as configuration which provides read-only/write many storages, and protected from deletion, even by highest level permissions or authorised personnel or backup vendor.

  • Access to backups is restricted to authorised personnel only, in line with ISP011-Information Access Rights Policy.pdf

  • Physical backup media (if used) must be stored in a secure, locked facility.

  • Offline backups must be digitally disconnected when not in use to prevent exposure.

This document meets the following clauses:

  • ISO/IEC 27002:2022 -- A.7.10 (Storage media) and A.7.14 (Secure disposal or re-use of equipment).

  • Electronic Communications (Security Measures) Regulations 2022 -- Regulation 4 (Protect stored data and functions) and Regulation 12 (Equipment upgrades, including EOL disposal).

Purpose: To securely dispose of or re-use media and equipment, preventing data leaks and reducing security risks.

docs.title: Scope
docs.text:
Applies to all media and equipment in our ISMS, including:

  • IT assets (e.g., servers, laptops, storage devices).

  • Network assets (e.g., routers, switches, base stations, customer equipment, SIM cards).

  • All storage types (e.g., hard drives, USBs, tapes, SSDs).

  • Assets with sensitive data, owned or managed by us or third parties.

docs.title: Procedures
docs.text:
All media and equipment must be inventoried per the Asset Management Policy.

  1. Prior to disposal or re-use, assess:

a) Data classification, does this device contain any Confidential or Strictly Confidential data (ISP037-Information Classification and Handling Policy).

b) Check and update asset inventory including device details, data, software, location.

  1. Storage media no longer required must be disposed of using formal procedures to prevent data recovery. This includes storage media contained within any hardware devices.

  2. Methods (selected based on data sensitivity and risk NIST.SP.800-88r1 ) :

    a) Clear: Overwrite data with non-sensitive info using standard tools (quick but basic protection).

    b) Purge: Use advanced erase commands (e.g., overwrite, block erase, or crypto erase) to make recovery impossible.

    c) Destroy: Physically break it down (e.g., shred, incinerate) if purge isn\'t possible.

  3. Save non-sensitive data securely first before disposing of storage media.

  4. Use tools to check data can\'t be recovered (e.g., random checks).

  5. Reset to factory settings; reconfigure securely.

  6. Destroy high-risk items physically.

  7. For network equipment, remove configs that could reveal secrets (e.g., passwords, keys).

  8. For off-site work; use certified vendors and get destruction certificates; keep records for 3+ years in asset system.

  9. Follow Incident Management Policy to report problems and incident.

docs.title: Hard copy (Paper)
docs.text:
• Clear/Purge: Not applicable.

  • Destroy: Shred with a crosscut shredder.

docs.title: Networking Devices (e.g., Routers, Switches)
docs.text:
• Clear: Do a full factory reset.

  • Purge: Usually not available; use destroy if needed. Check manufacturer for advanced erase.

  • Destroy: Shred, disintegrate, pulverise, or incinerate via certified vendor.

  • Notes: Remove removable storage first.

docs.title: Apple iPhone/iPad
docs.text:
• Clear/Purge: Use \"Erase All Content and Settings\" (Settings > General > Reset). Assumes encryption is on.

  • Destroy: Shred or incinerate via certified vendor.

  • Notes: Verify no data remains (check history, files). Backup first. Remote wipe is only a clear.

docs.title: Android Devices
docs.text:
• Clear: Factory reset via settings (e.g., Backup and Reset > Factory Data Reset).

  • Purge: Check manufacturer for secure erase or crypto erase; may vary.

  • Destroy: Shred or incinerate via certified vendor.

  • Notes: Verify no data remains. Use guides like DISA STIGs for setup. Remote wipe is only a clear.

docs.title: ATA Hard Drives
docs.text:
• Clear: Overwrite with a single pass of fixed data (e.g., zeros).

  • Purge: Use ATA sanitise commands (e.g., overwrite, crypto erase) or security erase.

  • Destroy: Shred or incinerate via certified vendor.

  • Notes: Verify after action. Backup first.

docs.title: ATA SSDs (PATA, SATA, etc.)
docs.text:
• Clear: Overwrite with one pass (may shorten device life); or use security erase.

  • Purge: Use block erase or crypto erase; verify.

  • Destroy: Shred or incinerate.

  • Notes: Reset hidden areas first. Not all encryption works for purge; check specs. No degaussing.

docs.title: SCSI SSDs (Parallel SCSI, SAS, etc.)
docs.text:
• Clear: Overwrite with one pass.

  • Purge: Use SCSI sanitise (block/crypto erase); or TCG interface for key change.

  • Destroy: Shred or incinerate.

  • Notes: Verify; reset configs. No degaussing.

docs.title: NVM Express SSDs
docs.text:
• Clear: Overwrite with one pass.

  • Purge: Use format command (user data or crypto erase); or TCG for key change.

  • Destroy: Shred or incinerate.

  • Notes: Verify; no degaussing.

docs.title: USB Removable Media (e.g., Thumb Drives)
docs.text:
• Clear: Overwrite with at least two passes (pattern + complement).

  • Purge: Often not supported; destroy instead.

  • Destroy: Shred or incinerate.

  • Notes: For high-risk, always destroy.

Report incidents (e.g., improper disposal leading to compromise) per the Incident Management Policy. ISD003-Incident Reporting and Management Framework.pdf

Term Description Reference

Asset Any item of value to the organisation, including information, hardware, software, facilities, and personnel.

Asset management Identifying and recording of an Asset management - organisation\'s physical assets, NCSC.GOV.UK software, data, essential staff and utilities.

docs.title: General Information
docs.text:
This document meets the following clauses:

  • Information Security Management System BS EN ISO/IEC 27002:2022 -- A 5.9 Inventory of information and other associated assets

  • Information Security Management System BS EN ISO/IEC 27002:2022 -- A 5.11 -- Return of Assets

  • The Electronic Communications (Security Measures) Regulations 2022: Regulation 6 (4): maintain records of the type, location, software and hardware information and identifying information of equipment.

docs.title: Scope
docs.text: This policy applies to all assets owned, used, or managed by Community Fibre within the information security management system scope. Assets include information, hardware, software, network equipment, data storage, virtualised environments, and people involved in network technology, operations, and field activities. It covers public electronic communications networks and services, including customer premises equipment, management planes, signalling planes, and supply chain components.

docs.title: Policy
docs.text:
All information assets shall be identified and documented in a central asset register. Asset registers shall include:

  • Identified assets relevant to the secure operation of essential function(s)

  • Inventories shall include suitable levels of detail e.g., location, hardware, software, firmware, supplier, EOL date.

  • Dependencies on supporting infrastructure (e.g. power, cooling etc)

  • Ownership and custodianship.

  • Assets relevant to security-critical functions or sensitive data shall be managed with cyber security in mind throughout their lifecycle, from creation through to eventual decommissioning or disposal.

  • New assets shall be added to the associated inventory before use.

  • Inventories shall be reviewed at least annually or following significant changes.

  • Asset management systems shall integrate with monitoring tools to detect anomalies and support threat hunting.

docs.title: Asset ownership
docs.text:
All information assets shall have a designated owner responsible for its lifecycle management, including assessing regulatory and data protection requirements and capabilities with support from associated suppliers and Security Operations.

Information asset owners shall:

  • Appropriately classification and protect assets in accordance with ISP037-Information Classification and Handling Policy and ISP043-Information Backup Policy .

  • Ensure proper handling when the asset is reused or disposed of in accordance with ISP044-Secure Disposal Policy.

  • Owners shall periodically assess risks, including those from incoming signals.

  • Periodically review access restrictions considering applicable access control policies and supply chain vulnerabilities.

docs.title: Classification of information assets
docs.text:
Information assets shall be classified based on sensitivity and criticality in line with the ISP037-Information Classification and Handling Policy:

  • Public: no restrictions.

  • Confidential: high value, requiring encryption and access controls.

  • Strictly Confidential: sensitive data or related to security-critical functions, with strict protections against compromises.

Classification shall consider regulatory definitions, such as sensitive data or content of signals. Assets shall be labelled accordingly, using electronic metadata or physical tags where applicable.

docs.title: Acceptable use and handling
docs.text:
Assets shall be used only for authorised purposes in line with the ISP030-Acceptable Use Policy

  • Prohibiting unauthorised modifications to network equipment or functions.

  • Ensuring secure protocols for management access, with multi-factor authentication.

  • Protecting assets from exposure to untrusted networks or incoming signals.

  • Handling sensitive data with encryption and monitoring for compromises.

Field operations teams shall follow secure procedures for asset deployment and maintenance, avoiding reliance on external persons or equipment where risks are identified.

docs.title: Return and disposal of assets
docs.text:
Upon termination of use, assets shall be returned or disposed of securely in line with ISP044-Secure Disposal Policy.

Procedures include:

  • Erasing sensitive data to prevent recovery.

  • Documenting disposal in the asset register.

  • For network equipment, ensuring no residual risks to operations.

docs.title: Document Objective
docs.text: The purpose of this document is to demonstrate the management board's commitment to Data Protection and to provide the over-arching policy statements to which all subordinate policies and controls must adhere.

docs.title: 1.2 References and Related Documents

2 **Information ISP003-Information Security Security Policy** Policy

This document meets the following clauses:

Information Security Management System BS EN ISO/IEC 27001:2022 -- A.5.34 Privacy and protection of PII

docs.title: Policy Overview
docs.text:
The Board of Directors and management of Community Fibre Limited are committed to compliance with, and the protection of the "rights and freedoms" of individuals whose information Community Fibre Limited collects and processes in accordance with the EU GDPR.

We are committed to preserving the confidentiality, integrity, and availability of all the physical and electronic information and information-related assets relevant to meet the purpose and goals of the organisation. This includes the handling of personal data or "Personally Identifiable Information" (PII).

Furthermore, we are committed to ensuring compliance with the European Union General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) and the UK Data Protection Act (DPA) 2018 and any other data protection legislation or regulation relevant to our business operations.

In complying with the above-mentioned legislation and regulation, the organisation makes commitments to implement policies and processes related to that compliance and to make staff and relevant third parties aware of their responsibilities when handling personal data.

More detailed policies and processes thus support this policy, including our Information Security Policy. A GDPR compliance workspace is also maintained in line with Information Commissioner Office recommendations. These are located and managed within the ISMS management platform (ISMS.online).

This policy will be reviewed regularly to respond to any changes in the business, its risk assessment or risk treatment plan, and at least annually.

docs.title: Scope
docs.text: All employees and relevant interested parties associated to the organisation's handling of personal data must comply with this policy. Appropriate training and materials to support it are available.

docs.title: Definitions
docs.text: The key definitions of terms used within or referred to by this policy are based upon those in the GDPR or other recognised documentation and are contained in Annex A.

docs.title: Organisational Responsibilities
docs.text:
Our Data Protection Officer has overall responsibility for the day-to-day implementation of this policy.

This policy will be reviewed regularly to respond to any changes in the business, its risk assessment or risk treatment plan, and at least annually.

docs.title: Staff data protection training
docs.text:
All staff will receive training on this policy. New joiners will receive training as part of the induction process. Further training will be provided at least every two years or whenever there is a substantial change in the law or our policy and procedure.

Training is provided on a regular basis and when specific trigger events occur e.g., threats or incidents affecting all or part of the organisation, its supply chain or other Interested Parties that might impact the organisation financially or reputationally.

It will cover:

  • The law relating to data protection.

  • Our data protection and related policies and procedures.

Completion of this training is compulsory and where appropriate will be evidenced by task completion on the ISMS.online platform.

docs.title: Privacy Notice -- transparency of data protection
docs.text: Being transparent and providing accessible information to individuals about how we will use their personal data is important for our organisation and is required under GDPR. Whenever personal data is being collected, we will document and provide a Privacy Notice in line with the requirements of Article 13 of the GDPR.

docs.title: Conditions for processing
docs.text: We will ensure any use of personal data is justified using at least one of the conditions for processing (described further below) and this will be specifically documented in the ISMS.online platform. All staff who are responsible for processing personal data will be aware of the conditions for processing. The conditions for processing will be available to data subjects in the form of a privacy notice.

docs.title: Justification for personal data
docs.text: We will process personal data in compliance with all eight data protection principles. We will identify all sensitive categories of data and document the additional justification for the processing of this data.

docs.title: Sensitive personal data
docs.text: In most cases where we process sensitive personal data, we will require the data subject\'s explicit consent to do this unless exceptional circumstances apply, or we are required to do this by law (e.g., to comply with legal obligations to ensure health and safety at work). Any such consent will need to identify clearly what the relevant data is, why it is being processed and to whom it will be disclosed.

docs.title: Fair and lawful processing
docs.text:
We must process personal data fairly and lawfully in accordance with individuals' rights. This generally means that we should not process personal data unless the individual whose details we are processing has consented to this happening.

Under GDPR, processing of personal data is lawful only if at least one of the following apply:

a) The data subject has given consent to the processing of his or her personal data for one or more specific purposes.

b) Processing is necessary for the performance of a contract to which the data subject is party or to take steps.

c) At the request of the data subject prior to entering into a contract.

d) Processing is necessary for compliance with a legal obligation to which the controller is subject.

e) Processing is necessary to protect the vital interests of the data subject or of another natural person.

f) Processing is necessary for the performance of a task carried out in the public interest or in the exercise of official.

g) Authority vested in the controller.

h) Processing is necessary for the purposes of the legitimate interests pursued by the controller or by a third party,

i) Except where such interests are overridden by the interests or fundamental rights and freedoms of the data subject which require protection of personal data, where the data subject is a child.

docs.title: The processing of all personal data must be:
docs.text:
• Necessary to deliver our services.

  • In our legitimate interests and not unduly prejudice the individual\'s privacy.

  • In most cases this provision will apply to routine business data processing activities.

Our Terms of Business contain a Privacy Notice to clients on data protection. The notice:

  • Sets out the purposes for which we hold personal data on customers and employees.

  • Highlights that our work may require us to give information to third parties such as expert witnesses and other professional advisers.

  • Provides those customers have a right of access to the personal data that we hold about them.

docs.title: Consent
docs.text: The data that we collect is subject to active consent by the data subject. This consent can be revoked at any time.

docs.title: Accuracy and relevance
docs.text:
We will ensure that any personal data we process is accurate, adequate, relevant, and not excessive, given the purpose for which it was obtained. We will not process personal data obtained for one purpose for any unconnected purpose unless the individual concerned has agreed to this or would otherwise reasonably expect this.

Individuals may ask that we correct inaccurate personal data relating to them. If you believe that information is inaccurate, you should record the fact that the accuracy of the information is in dispute and inform the Data Protection Officer.

docs.title: Data Portability
docs.text:
Upon request, a data subject should have the right to receive a copy of their data in a structured format. These requests should be processed within one month, provided there is no undue burden, and it does not compromise the privacy of other individuals.

A data subject may also request that their data is transferred directly to another system. This must be done for free.

docs.title: Right to be forgotten
docs.text: A data subject may request that any information held on them is deleted or removed, and any third parties who process or use that data must also comply with the request. An erasure request can only be refused if an exemption applies.

docs.title: Privacy by design and default
docs.text:
Privacy by design is an approach to projects that promote privacy and data protection compliance from the start. The Data Protection Officer will be responsible for conducting Privacy Impact Assessments (PIA) and ensuring that all IT and other relevant projects commence with a privacy plan.

The standard operating procedure for data protection by design and default [3] is maintained by the Data Protection Officer.

When relevant, and when it does not have a negative impact on the data subject, privacy settings will be set to the most private by default.

docs.title: International data transfers
docs.text: No data may be transferred outside of the EEA without first discussing it with the data protection officer. Specific consent from the data subject must be obtained prior to transferring their data outside the EEA.

docs.title: Data security
docs.text:
We must keep personal data secure against loss or misuse. Where other organisations process personal data as a service on our behalf, the Data Protection Officer will establish what, if any, additional specific data security arrangements need to be implemented in contracts with those third-party organisations.

The organisation has a documented Information Security Policy [2] and a set of subordinate security policies and controls relating to our management of data and information security. These are held within the ISMS.online platform.

docs.title: Data retention
docs.text:
We must not retain personal data for longer than is necessary. What is "necessary" will depend on the circumstances of each case, considering the reasons that the personal data was obtained, but should be determined in a manner consistent with our data retention guidelines.

Data retention schedules will be maintained showing the minimum and maximum periods of retention for each data set.

docs.title: Data audit and register
docs.text: Regular (at least annual) data audits to manage and mitigate risks will inform the data register. This contains information on what data is held, where it is stored, how it is used, who is responsible and any further regulations or retention timescales that may be relevant.

docs.title: Staff Responsibilities
docs.text:
All individual staff members are responsible for playing their part in maintaining the confidentiality, integrity, and availability of personal data in compliance with the GDPR, DPA and organisational policies, standards, and procedures.

You must familiarise yourself with the requirements contained in this policy and any other relevant security policy and comply with any requirements relating to the proper handling and security of personal data.

docs.title: Your personal data
docs.text: You must take reasonable steps to ensure that personal data we hold about you is accurate and updated as required. For example, if your personal circumstances change, please inform the Data Protection Officer or the HR Department so that they can update your records.

docs.title: Handling others' personal data
docs.text: You must familiarise yourself with the organisational responsibilities detailed above and ensure that you comply with these whenever you are handling personal data. Special care and attention must be given when handling sensitive personal data.

docs.title: Processing data in accordance with the individual\'s rights
docs.text:
You must abide by any request from an individual not to use their personal data for direct marketing purposes. Notify the Data Protection Officer about any such request if it falls outside of the normal processes or you have any reason to be unsure about the appropriate practice.

Contact the Data Protection Officer for advice on direct marketing before starting any new direct marketing activity to ensure compliance with all relevant data protection and other legislation.

docs.title: Reporting breaches
docs.text:
All members of staff have an obligation to report actual or potential data protection weaknesses, events, and incidents where compliance may be breached. This allows us to:

  • Investigate the failure and take remedial steps if necessary.

  • Maintain a register of compliance failures.

  • Notify the Supervisory Authority (SA) of any compliance failures that are material either or part of a pattern of failures.

The reporting of such weaknesses, events and incidents will be managed through our Information Security Incident Management processes.

docs.title: Monitoring
docs.text: Everyone must observe this policy. The Data Protection Officer has overall responsibility for this policy. They will monitor it regularly to make sure it is being adhered to.

docs.title: Annex A -- Key Definitions
docs.text:
Data Subject "Data subject" means an individual who is the subject of personal data; [source DPA 2018]

Personal Data "Personal Data" is any information relating to an identified or identifiable natural person ('data subject'). An identifiable natural person is one who can be identified, directly or indirectly, by reference to an identifier such as a name, an identification number, location data, an online identifier or to one or more factors specific to the physical, physiological, genetic, mental, economic, cultural or social identity of that natural person. [source GDPR]

Sensitive Personal "Sensitive Personal Data" is any information about an Data individual\'s racial or ethnic origin, political opinions, religious or similar beliefs, trade union membership (or non-membership), physical or mental health or condition, criminal offences, or related proceedings---any use of sensitive personal data should be strictly controlled in accordance with this policy. [source DPA 2018]

Controller "Controller" means the natural or legal person, public authority, agency, or other body which, alone or jointly with others, determines the purposes and means of the processing of personal data. Where the purposes and means of such processing are determined by Union or Member State law, the controller or the specific criteria for its nomination may be provided for by Union or Member State law. [source GDPR]

Processor "Processor" means a natural or legal person, public authority, agency, or other body, which processes personal data on behalf of the controller. [source GDPR]

Recipient "Recipient" means a natural or legal person, public authority, agency, or another body, to which the personal data are disclosed, whether a third party or not. However, public authorities which may receive personal data in the framework of a particular inquiry in accordance with Union or Member State law shall not be regarded as recipients. The processing of those data by those public authorities shall be in compliance with the applicable data protection rules according to the purposes of the processing. [source GDPR]

Processing "Processing" means any operation or set of operations which is performed on personal data or on sets of personal data, whether or not by automated means, such as collection, recording, organisation, structuring, storage, adaptation or alteration, retrieval, consultation, use, disclosure by transmission, dissemination or otherwise making available, alignment or combination, restriction, erasure or destruction. [source GDPR]

Profiling "Profiling" means any form of automated processing of personal data consisting of the use of personal data to evaluate certain personal aspects relating to a natural person, to analyse or predict aspects concerning that natural person\'s performance at work, economic situation, health, personal preferences, interests, reliability, behaviour, location or movements. [source GDPR]

Pseudonymisation "Pseudonymisation" means the processing of personal data in such a manner that the personal data can no longer be attributed to a specific data subject without the use of additional information, provided that such additional information is kept separately and is subject to technical and organisational measures to ensure that the personal data are not attributed to an identified or identifiable natural person. [source GDPR]

Filing System "Filing system" means any structured set of personal data which is accessible according to specific criteria, whether centralised, decentralised or dispersed on a functional or geographical basis. [source GDPR]

Consent "Consent" of the data subject means any freely given, specific, informed, and unambiguous indication of the data subject\'s wishes by which he or she, by a statement or by a clear affirmative action, signifies agreement to the processing of personal data relating to him or her. [source GDPR]

Personal Data "Personal data breach" means a breach of security Breach leading to the accidental or unlawful destruction, loss, alteration, unauthorised disclosure of, or access to, personal data transmitted, stored, or otherwise processed. [source GDPR]

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text: This Legitimate Interest Policy outlines the framework under which Community Fibre Limited processes personal data based on the legal basis of \"Legitimate Interests\" as per the Data Protection Act 2018 and the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR).

docs.title: Scope
docs.text: This policy applies to all personal data processed by Community Fibre Limited and its subsidiaries, where the legal basis for such processing is legitimate interest.

docs.title: Definitions
docs.text:
• Personal Data: Any information relating to an identified or identifiable natural person.

  • Processing: Any operation performed on personal data, whether automated or not.

  • Legitimate Interests: A legal basis for processing personal data, other than consent, contract, or legal obligation

docs.title: Identification of Legitimate Interests
docs.text:
Before processing any personal data based on legitimate interests, [Your Company Name] will:

  • Clearly identify the legitimate interests pursued.

  • Conduct a Legitimate Interests Assessment (LIA) to ensure that these interests are not overridden by the data subject's interests, rights, or freedoms.

docs.title: Legitimate Interests Assessment (LIA)
docs.text:
The LIA will include:

  • Purpose Test: Identify the legitimate interest behind the processing.

  • Necessity Test: Ensure that the processing is necessary to achieve the identified interests.

  • Balancing Test: Ensure that the legitimate interests are not overridden by the data subject\'s interests, rights, or freedoms.

docs.title: Data Minimization
docs.text: Community Fibre Limited will only process data that is strictly necessary for the identified legitimate interests.

docs.title: Transparency
docs.text: Data subjects will be informed about the processing activities based on legitimate interests through privacy notices or other appropriate means.

docs.title: Data Subject Rights
docs.text: Data subjects have the right to object to processing based on legitimate interests. Upon receiving an objection, [Your Company Name] will immediately cease processing unless it can demonstrate compelling legitimate grounds for the processing.

docs.title: Record-keeping
docs.text: All LIAs and related documentation will be kept on record and made available for inspection by regulatory authorities.

docs.title: This policy will be reviewed at least annually or whenever there is a significant change in processing activities.

docs.title: Scope
docs.text:
All personal data processed by Community Fibre is within the scope of this procedure.

Data subjects are entitled to obtain the following:

  • Confirmation as to whether Community Fibre is processing any personal data about that individual.

  • Access to their personal data.

  • Any related information.

docs.title: Responsibilities
docs.text:
1. The Data Protection Officer is responsible for the application and effective working of this procedure, and for reporting to the information owner Chief Information Officer on subject access requests (SARs).

    2. The Data Protection Officer is responsible for handling all SARs.

docs.title: Procedure
docs.text:
1. SARs are made using the Subject Access Request Record.

    2. The data subject provides Community Fibre with evidence of their identity, in the form of a current passport/driving license, and the signature on the identity must be cross-checked to that on the application form (Subject Access Request Record).

    3. The data subject identifies the specific set of data held by Community Fibre on their SAR. The data subject can request all data held on them.

    4. Community Fibre records the date that the identification checks were conducted, and the specification of the data sought.

    5. Community Fibre provides the requested information to the data subject within one month from this recorded date.

    6. Once received, the SAR application is immediately forwarded to the Data Protection Officer, who will ensure that the requested data is collected within the specified time frame in Clause 3.5 above. Collection entails:

      1. Collecting the data specified by the data subject.

      2. Searching all databases and all relevant filing systems (manual files) in Community Fibre, including all backup and archived files (computerised or manual) and all email folders and archives. The Data Protection Officer maintains a data map that identifies where all data in Community Fibre is stored in ISMS.online

    7. The Data Protection Officer maintains a record of requests for data and of its receipt, including dates in ISMS.online.

    8. The Data Protection Officer reviews SARs from a child. Before responding to a SAR of the child data subject, the Data Protection Officer considers their ability to make the request by adequately explaining any implications of sharing their personal data.

    9. The Data Protection Officer reviews all documents that have been provided to identify whether any third parties are present in it, and either removes the identifying third-party information from the documentation or obtains written consent from the third party for their identity to be revealed.

    10. If any of the requested data is being held or processed under one of the following exemptions, it does not have to be provided:

  2. National security

  3. Crime and taxation

  4. Health

  5. Regulatory activity

  6. Publicly available information

  7. Corporate finance

  8. Confidential references

  9. Management forecasts

  10. Legal advice and proceedings

  11. If a data subject requests Community Fibre to provide them with the personal data stored by the controller/processor, then Community Fibre will provide the data subject with the requested information in electronic format, unless otherwise specified. All the items provided to the data subject are listed in Records of Processing Activity (ROPA) hosted in ISMS.online, which shows the data subject's name and the date on which the information is delivered to the data subject.

  12. If a data subject requests what personal data is being processed, then Community Fibre provides the data subject with the following information:

    1. Purpose of the processing.

    2. Categories of personal data.

    3. Recipient(s) of the information, including recipients in third countries or international organisations.

    4. How long the personal data will be stored.

    5. The data subject's right to request rectification or erasure, restriction, or objection, relative to their personal data being processed.

    6. Community Fibre removes personal data from systems and processing operations as soon as a request for erasure has been submitted by the data subject.

    7. Community Fibre contacts and communicates via email with other organisations, where the personal data of the data subject is being processed, to cease processing information at the request of the data subject.

    8. Community Fibre takes appropriate measures without undue delay if the data subject has withdrawn consent or objects to the processing of their personal data in whole or part; or Community Fibre is no longer under legal obligation; and/or the personal data has been unlawfully processed.

    9. Inform the data subject of their right to lodge a complaint with the supervisory authority and a method to do so.

    10. Information on the source of the personal data if it has not been collected from the data subject.

    11. Information about any automated decision-making.

    12. If and where personal data has been transferred and information on any safeguards in place.

  13. Community Fibre uses the following electronic formats to respond to SARs: common machine-readable formats including Microsoft Office documents, Adobe PDF's, and .mp3 audio files.

docs.title: General Information
docs.text: The purpose of this document is to define the GDPR compliance policies and procedures for Community Fibre. It defines the scope under GDPR in terms of lawfulness, fairness, transparency, purpose limitation, data minimisation, accuracy, storage limitation, integrity, confidentiality, and accountability. It addresses compliance with legal obligations under ISO 27001 clause A.5.31, ensuring data protection practices are compliant and properly managed.

docs.title: Scope
docs.text: The scope of GDPR compliance for CFL is structured around seven key principles as outlined by GDPR experts:

docs.title: 1. Lawfulness, fairness, and transparency
docs.text:
Whenever you're processing personal data, you should have a good reason for doing so. GDPR terms this principle as lawfulness. Reasons for processing data can include:

  1. The user has given you consent to do so.

  2. You must do it to make good on a contract.

  3. It's necessary to fulfil a legal obligation.

  4. For protection of vital interests of a natural person.

  5. It's a public task done in public interest.

  6. You can prove you have legitimate interest, and it's not overridden by data subject's rights and interests.

The concept of fairness laid out in the GDPR goes hand-in-hand with lawfulness. It means you shouldn't purposely withhold information about what or why you're collecting data. In other words, users wouldn't be surprised if they knew how you were using their data. Fairness means you won't mishandle or misuse the data you collect. We must record the rationale.

Transparency is inherently linked to fairness: Being clear, open, and honest with data subjects about who you are, and why and how you're processing their personal data is the definition of transparency. By following it, you act fairly towards your data subjects.

docs.title: 2. Purpose limitation
docs.text:
The GDPR's second principle sets boundaries around using data only for specific activities. This purpose limitation means data is "collected for specified, explicit, and legitimate purposes" only, as stated in the GDPR.

Your purposes for processing data must be clearly established. And they must also be clearly communicated to individuals through a privacy notice. Finally, you must follow them closely, limiting the processing of data to only the purposes you've stated.

If at any point, you want to use the data you've collected for a new purpose that's incompatible with your original purpose, you must ask specifically for consent again to do it --- unless you have a clear obligation or function set out in law.

docs.title: 3. Data minimisation
docs.text: Only collect the smallest amount of data you'll need to complete your purposes. This is the GDPR principle of data minimisation. For example, if you want to gather subscribers for your email newsletter, you should only ask for information necessary to send out the newsletters. Avoid gathering personal data such as phone numbers or home addresses, which aren't directly related to your purpose.

docs.title: 4. Accuracy
docs.text: It's up to you to ensure the accuracy of the data you collect and store. Set up checks and balances to correct, update, or erase incorrect or incomplete data that comes in. Also have regular audits on the calendar to double-check the cleanliness of stored data.

docs.title: 5. Storage limitations
docs.text: According to the GDPR, you must justify the length of time you're keeping each piece of data you store. Data retention periods are a good thing to establish to meet this storage limitation policy. Create a standard period after which you'll anonymise any data you're not actively using.

docs.title: 6. Integrity and confidentiality
docs.text: The GDPR requires you maintain the integrity and confidentiality of the data you collect, essentially keeping it secure from internal or external threats. This takes planning and proactive diligence. You must protect data from unauthorised or unlawful processing and accidental loss, destruction, or damage.

docs.title: 7. Accountability
docs.text: The GDPR regulators know an organisation can say they're following all the rules without doing it. That's why they require a level of accountability: You must have appropriate measures and records in place as proof of your compliance with the data processing principles.  Supervisory authorities can ask for this evidence at any time. Documentation is key here. It creates an audit trail you --- and authorities --- can follow if you do need to prove responsibility.

docs.title: Management and organisational records management
docs.text:
1. Records management organisation - Your business has defined and allocated records management responsibilities.

  2. Records management policy - Your business has approved and published an appropriate records management policy. This is subject to a regular review process.

  3. Records management risk - Your business has identified records management risks as part of a wider information risk management process.

  4. Records management training - Your business incorporates records management within a formal training programme. This comprises mandatory training with regular refresher material, and specialist training for those with specific records management functions.

  5. Monitoring and reporting - Your business carries out periodic checks on records security and there is monitoring of compliance with records management procedures.

docs.title: Records creation and maintenance
docs.text:
1. Record creation - Your business has set minimum standards for the creation of paper or electronic records.

  2. Information you hold - Your business has identified where you use manual and electronic records keeping systems and actively maintains a centralised record of those systems.

  3. Information standards - Your business has processes in place to ensure that the personal data you collect is accurate, adequate, relevant and not excessive. You carry out regular reviews to remove any personal data or records that are out of date or no longer relevant.

docs.title: Tracking and offsite storage
docs.text:
1. Tracking and offsite storage of paper records - Your business has tracking mechanisms to record the movement of manual records and ensure their security between office and storage areas and in instances where records are taken offsite.

  2. Offsite transfer of electronic records - Your business has appropriate measures in place to transfer of electronic records off-site and protect personal data from loss or theft.

  3. Secure storage of records - Your business stores paper and electronic records securely with appropriate environmental controls and higher levels of security around special categories of personal data.

docs.title: Access to records
docs.text:
1. Access to records - Your business restricts access to records storage areas to prevent unauthorised access, damage, theft or loss. You should implement role-based access and check it regularly.

  2. Your business has a process to assign and manage user accounts to authorised individuals and to remove them when it is no longer appropriate.

  3. Business continuity - Your business has business continuity plans in place in the event of a disaster. This includes identifying records that are critical to the continued functioning or reconstitution of your business. You also routinely back up data that is stored electronically to help restore information if needed.

  4. Disposal of data - Your business has a retention and disposal schedule which details how long you will keep manual and electronic records.

  5. Your business has confidential waste disposal processes to ensure that records are destroyed to an appropriate standard.

docs.title: Data security controls
docs.text:
• Use of the Island browser for critical applications such as HOBS will become mandatory. This will enable better protection of the data and a full audit trail to show downloads from the core platforms and prevents data from being transferred to unapproved (i.e. private) cloud services. (i.e. Gmail, WhatsApp)

  • All company laptop and mobile storage are encrypted via configuration policy.

  • Microsoft Cloud App Security policies are configured to prevent access to corporate services from unauthorised devices except via a browser (i.e. Edge, Chrome) but this only applies to Microsoft services. These will be replaced with Island enforcement.

  • Microsoft Intune application policies prevent access to corporate services from personal mobile devices without enrolment and management of apps (i.e. Outlook, Teams, OneDrive, etc.)

  • Microsoft 365 Purview (Data Security) data loss policies currently monitor outbound email for data containing names and addresses. Thresholds for data loss alerts are configured (more than 50 names or addresses) which routes outbound email to quarantine.

  • Writing to USB storage devices is blocked via companywide policy. An exceptions list is maintained for field and network engineers that require USB storage for configuration of network equipment.

  • Where data is stored in Domo, the owner of the source data shall be responsible for the downstream data retention policy.

  • Backup policy to be checked and backups audited to ensure they do not contravene the system policy.

docs.title: Data masking (new requirement -- added 25/09)
docs.text:
To enhance data protection and comply with GDPR principles, particularly data minimisation, integrity, and confidentiality, Community Fibre implements data masking requirements for handling personal data in non-production environments, such as development, testing, and analytics.

Data masking involves obscuring or anonymising sensitive personal information to prevent unauthorised access or exposure while maintaining data utility for legitimate purposes.

Requirements for Data masking:

  1. Identification of Strictly Confidential data: All personal data elements (e.g., names, addresses, email addresses, phone numbers, financial details) must be identified and classified as sensitive prior to any masking activities. This classification shall align with GDPR definitions of personal data and special categories of data.

  2. Masking techniques: Appropriate masking methods must be applied based on data type and use case:

    a. Static Masking: Replace sensitive data with fixed fictional values (e.g., replace real names with \"John Doe\").

    b. Dynamic Masking: Mask data in real-time during access, ensuring original data remains unchanged in storage.

    c. Tokenisation: Substitute sensitive data with non-sensitive equivalents (tokens) that can be mapped back only by authorised systems.

    d. Anonymisation: Irreversibly alter data so it cannot be linked back to individuals, used when data is no longer needed in identifiable form.

  3. Scope of Application: Data masking is mandatory for:

    a. All personal data transferred to or used in non-production (i.e. Dev, UAT, SIT) environments.

    b. Third-party sharing where full data is not required (e.g., analytics or testing with vendors).

  4. Implementation and Controls:

    a. Automated tools (e.g., integrated into AWS, Asure, or other infrastructure) shall be used for masking to ensure consistency and reduce human error.

    b. Access to unmasked data is restricted to production environments and authorised personnel only, with role-based access controls (RBAC).
